en: In the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, it says:
"The seed is like a swan drinking milk.
The root treatise states: "Just as in the world, when one becomes free from desire, the permeations (*vāsanā*) of the non-tranquil stages are extinguished."
The meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) serves as an illustration of the supramundane transformation of the basis.

This [transformation] merely takes the sense of the prior stage’s increase in power and decrease in capacity as its meaning; it does not yet attain the state of a body that resembles the transformation of the basis through thorough penetration, which is characterized by permanence.
This is different from what follows.

As for the "basis" upon which the Sage relies: it is the fusion of the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) with the nature of understanding; taking this as the basis, all noble paths arise in dependence upon it.

This tenth [stage] clarifies that when one attains the nature of understanding impermanence through the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) which perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), one is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

After the perfuming has increased further, one subsequently ascends to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to establish the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), which is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); only then is one a noble one (*ārya*).
Therefore, it is said that the paths of all noble ones rely upon this.
Question:
Regarding the nature of understanding (jñatā) perfumed by the seeds of hearing and reflection—
There are those who explain, saying:
"This is the truly pure Dharma-body;
how can it be said to be an impermanent phenomenon?"
Answer:
That [response] was merely the idle chatter of one who has returned to the consciousness of the self, whose mind is discriminating and obscured.
This interpretation does not accord with the meaning.
The eternally abiding dharmas do not possess the quality of impermanence such that they could be perfumed;

rather, it is the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) that can perfume the subsequent sixth consciousness, which then becomes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), at which point it first constitutes the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
These seeds produced by hearing and reflection give rise to the objects of consciousness-only and to contemplative wisdom;
at that time, these are all in the sense of being the causes of all phenomena, which is the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Later, when afflictions are completely severed and the basis is transformed, the fruit of liberation is realized.
Only when the body [attains] the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) does it become the Dharma-body;
thus, the meaning of the true, pure mind as the Dharma-body refers both to the qualities of the fruit and to the qualities of the cause.

Furthermore, when the seeds of hearing and reflection combine to produce the noble one’s reliance upon the path of the noble ones, at the moment of correspondence with the Dharma-body of the cause, it consists solely of the qualities of the fruit based upon the Dharma-body.
There is no further sense of it being a causal seed.
The *Śāstra* states: "This chapter further cites [examples] that do not contradict reason to demonstrate that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) truly exists.
From here below, the meaning of the sixth chapter, "Conformity to Reason," is explained.
This means that the principle of the cessation of mental activity (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is established as logical precisely because of this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
This chapter consists of two parts:
first, it clarifies that the doctrine of the cessation of mental activity cannot be established without the fundamental consciousness.

Second, explaining that the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is not established in the absence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). This section consists of three parts:
first, a brief indication of the definitive characteristics to clarify the intent regarding gain and loss;
second, presenting the doctrines of the Hīnayāna to formally refute their errors.
Because the three fetters do not depart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), neither pure nor impure categories of phenomena are established therein.
This initial section is further divided into three parts:
first, the presentation of the primary characteristics; second, the exposition of the faults.
The three meditative absorptions (samāpatti) are not separate from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
This is indicated in the root treatise and can be seen elsewhere;
it is not explicitly explained there. The Commentary states: "In order to attain a state of peaceful abiding and to avoid the fault of falling away."
This clarifies the intended purpose.
Regarding the entry into meditative concentration, the activities are identical to those of a noble one practicing the attainment of cessation for two reasons:
first, to attain a dwelling in personal tranquility and bliss.
Having already attained the superior untainted dharmas,
one should now abide in the peaceful and blissful dwelling;
yet this concentration is devoid of the six consciousnesses.
It is similar to nirvāṇa in its tranquility and bliss;
therefore, the noble ones cultivate this concentration.
Second, it is for the sake of avoiding the fault of falling away.

When the six consciousnesses take objects as their conditions, they can give rise to improper mental application (ayoniśomanasikāra), which in turn produces various habitual tendencies (vāsanā) and afflictions (kleśa), leading to the loss of meditative concentration.
Fearing such loss, one cultivates the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) says: It is not that the substance of the mind itself is called "extinguished"; rather, it is called "extinguished" because the mental factors (citta-dharma) are extinguished.

Since the name "mind" is established based on its dependence upon what it relies upon (the mental factors), the following section [2] presents the Sautrāntika position to refute its faults and establish the *mūlavijñāna* (root-consciousness).
This text states that the Mahāsāṃghika school asserts:
"The meditative absorption of cessation does not cause the extinction of the substance; it is the mental factors that are extinguished.
Consciousness is the substance of the mind."
Feeling, perception, and mental formations are mental factors;
mental factors are the dependent,
while the substance of the mind is the basis.
Because the name "mind" is established based on its dependence upon the supported [mental factors],
it is said that "the mind is extinguished.
In reality, it is the mental factors that are extinguished, not the essence of the mind itself.
This will be refuted correctly below.
As for why it is necessary to eliminate mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), they say:
The reason one must extinguish mental factors is that a person who enters this meditative absorption must necessarily have attained the states of the two higher realms.
In the four dhyānas of the form realm, feeling serves as the repository.
It is also said that they take feeling as their reality;
therefore, pleasure extends to the third dhyāna, while equanimity pervades the fourth dhyāna.
In the formless realms, perception is the treasury.
This is also true:
because the perception of formless [realms] involves coarse movement, feeling is transformed into perception;
for feeling is the root of the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is destroyed by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the root of the afflictions destroyed by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
because feeling (*vedanā*) and mind (*citta*) arise in dependence upon dull objects.
Therefore, these are the fundamental afflictions to be eliminated by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Because perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are sharp, they are capable of inferential reasoning and seeking the principles;
therefore, these are the fundamental afflictions to be eliminated by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, one contemplates that sensation (*vedanā*) is the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*),
and perception (*saṃjñā*) is the root of all suffering.
The noble ones, seeing the faults inherent in sensation and perception, contemplate them and are thus able to extinguish sensation and perception.
Since sensation and perception have already ceased,
and mental formations do not arise either,
the mind that emerges from this meditative absorption is thus produced once again.
Therefore, it is said that consciousness does not depart from the body.
As for why consciousness is severed yet one does not die:
it is because life-span (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) maintain it, whereby death does not occur.
The Commentary states: "If a person enters the fourth dhyāna, bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*) are then severed.
Inhalation and exhalation constitute bodily formations;
because the body possesses inhalation and exhalation, the body does not die and is able to perform activities such as movement.
Furthermore, because breath arises from the body, it is called "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṃskāra*).

The Commentary states: "If, when a person enters the second dhyāna and so forth, speech is severed, it is because applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the basis of speech."
Because they give rise to verbal activities, they are called "mental formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Since both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) no longer exist from the second dhyāna upward,
it is said that "verbal formations have ceased."
The Commentary says: "If a person enters the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), mental formations (citta-saṃskāra) are then severed.
Here, mental factors (caitasika-dharma) are termed "mental formations" because they are able to perform the functions of the mind; thus they are called mental formations.
If the mind were merely the mind itself, devoid of attention (*manasikāra*) and phenomena such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*), it would have no capacity for action.
It is because attention, feeling, perception, and other such phenomena move within the mind that various functions arise.
Therefore, mental factors such as sensation and perception are called "mental formations" (*citta-saṃskāra*).
Since these mental factors no longer exist within the meditative absorption of the cessation of mind,
it is said that "mental formations have ceased."
The Commentary says: "In this way, when bodily formations cease, the body does not perish; mental formations should likewise be understood.
As for the statement that 'when mental formations cease, the mind does not perish,' the opponent contrasts this with bodily formations."
In the fourth dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), although inhalation and exhalation are severed, the physical body (*rūpakāya*) does not perish.
Why, then, is it not stated that while mental factors (*cittadharma*) are severed, the mind (*citta*) does not perish?
This statement still establishes the first position; however, the intention behind it will be refuted later by the author himself.
The commentary states: "Therefore, there is no further sense of emerging from meditative absorption or of consciousness arising again.
This means that within meditative absorption there is no consciousness;
since consciousness has been extinguished without remainder.
How can there be the meaning of emerging from meditative absorption and being reborn?
If that were so, one who enters meditative absorption would immediately enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, if there were actual cessation followed by rebirth, [this would contradict the nature of reality].
Then it would follow that even those who have attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and entered nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) would be born again.
The Commentary states: "If one were to exclude the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as established by the characteristics previously set forth.
Previously, the fundamental consciousness was established by means of three meanings.
That is to say: the characteristic of essence, the characteristic of cause, and the characteristic of fruit.
Without these three, nothing at all would be established.

The Commentary states: "If they were not mutually inseparable, then the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-samāpatti*) as well as the attainment of the cessation of mind (*citta-nirodha-samāpatti*) could not be established at all."
The following ten points refute the second section of the Hīnayāna [position].
Feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) are necessarily inseparable from the mind (citta),
just as the four great elements (mahābhūta) and their derivative matter (upādāyarūpa) are necessarily inseparable.
If the mind were not extinguished, then feeling, perception, and so forth would likewise not be extinguished;
thus, the meditative absorption of the extinction of the mind would not be established.
This is, for example, like the fact that mental factors such as feeling and perception cannot exist independently of one another.

The Commentary states: Regarding the statement that "the mental consciousness may be with conceptualization or without conceptualization," the mental consciousness being without conceptualization refers to the direct realization of the object, as in the stage of Patience (kṣānti) and beyond; because one has already abandoned [discursive] recitation and is called "one who realizes the principle through resemblance," it is termed "without conceptualization."

The Commentary states: "That which is manifested as the basis for the arising [of the mind]" means that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) has the function of serving as the basis for the mind emerging from meditative absorption;
this clarifies that this consciousness of absorption does not depart from the body.

The Commentary says: If one maintains that when this concentration arises there is another consciousness produced—meaning, if one holds that apart from the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), other six consciousnesses arise without being separated from the three natures—the Commentary says:

If it is argued that concentration is said to be wholesome because the concentrated mind is wholesome, this meaning is not correct; for it is not your own position that [concentration] is associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment (*alobha*), and this logical consequence must follow.
That position also does not admit that the meditative attainment of cessation possesses wholesome roots such as non-attachment (*alobha*) and so forth.
If you claim that the mind in this attainment is wholesome,
then it must necessarily be associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment.
Because there is no wholesome root of non-attachment apart from the wholesome mind alone.
Question:
To which nature does the essence of this meditative absorption belong?
Answer:
The essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is wholesome (*kuśala*);
however, it is not a wholesome mind or mental factor (*caitta*), because it is not [of the nature of] mind.
Question:
To which of the four kinds of wholesomeness does it belong? Answer: [It belongs to] wholesome action born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-kuśala*).
It belongs to the category of initiating the wholesome.
By means of the seeds produced by the path of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it obstructs the mind so that [unwholesome states] do not arise;
that which can obstruct the seeds is the very essence of meditative concentration.
It is called "virtue of origination" because it is initiated by skillful means.
Regarding the four kinds of virtue:
first is true virtue.
It is precisely nirvāṇa.
Second, it is wholesome by nature;
that is, the wholesome roots such as non-attachment and so forth.
Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is wholesome,
the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are mixed with the wholesome;
these are the remaining mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
This is because they arise in association with the universal characteristics of the wholesome mental consciousness.
Fourth is "initiating wholesomeness," which refers to the wholesomeness of body and speech.
It becomes wholesome because it is initiated by mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Regarding the essential nature of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the treatise defines its essence as the seeds produced by the path of concentration.
Both the path and these seeds are capable of obstructing the mind and mental factors that are about to arise, preventing them from coming into existence.
The path arises and then immediately passes away.
At the time of entering meditative absorption, there are only the seeds produced by the path that adhere to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) without being extinguished;
this is described as the essence of the absorption.
It is called "arousing the wholesome" because it is produced by the path of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mārga*).

Later, upon emerging from concentration or when regressing or progressing, one again employs these seeds to cultivate the path of concentration within a defiled mind; thus, when the mind arises, it is more tranquil and superior than the mind at the previous time.
The Commentary on the Śāstra states: "A wholesome mind is pervasive and has no distinctions, because all mental factors (caitta-dharma) are inseparable from one another.
This means that when the mind arises, it is accompanied by these mental factors; because they are wholesome, it is said to be "pervasive."
The Commentary says: If they were not dissociated, then feeling, perception, and so forth would likewise not cease; therefore, it is impossible to establish this mind as virtuous.
If a virtuous mind arises, it necessarily arises together with all the mental factors.
Since a wholesome mind exists, there must necessarily be mental factors such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth.
Because such faults would follow, it is impossible to establish that a wholesome mind [exists independently].
The Commentary states: "When one becomes detached from the desire realm, all unwholesome states are extinguished; therefore, it is not of an unwholesome nature."
In the two higher realms, there is no longer any evil nature.
One who attains the meditative absorption of cessation must first attain the meditative absorptions of the two higher realms;
how could there be any evil within such absorptions?

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "It must necessarily be associated with the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and it should also necessarily be associated with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
This treats feeling and perception as being simultaneous.
If this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is a wholesome dharma (*kuśaladharma*), it must necessarily be associated with the roots of goodness.
If this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is necessarily mental, it must be associated with mental factors (*caitasika*).

The *Śāstra* states: "There is no distinct causal condition for establishing this absorption such that it would be associated only with the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), while there is a distinct causal condition for not establishing it as being associated with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)."
One might say that there is the meaning of association and non-association;
yet, since there is no distinct causal condition [for such a distinction],
how could one maintain such a dogmatic adherence?
The Commentary states: "As for the statement that this meaning is not established," this further clarifies the sense of its non-establishment;
this phrase first sets forth the meaning.
The Commentary states: "That which is to be countered exists, and that which counters it also exists.
This sentence serves as proof that the [opponent's] position is not established.
That which is to be countered consists of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
Perception and feeling exist;
this meditative concentration is their antidote.
When the fundamental consciousness ceases, perception ceases.
Since the perception still persists,
how could this meditative absorption of the cessation of mind exist? Therefore,
the definition [of this state] is not established.
The *Śāstra* states: "For example, when desire and so forth are arising, [the cultivation of] the contemplation of impurity and so forth cannot exist.
This sentence serves as an analogy and proof for the principle that the counteractive agent (*pratipakṣa*) and the object to be countered (*vipakṣa*) do not arise simultaneously.
If desire, anger, and so forth are currently manifesting, the contemplation of impurity and the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion can certainly not manifest.
As long as the ideation of craving persists,
that which is to be counteracted is present.
The meditative absorption of the cessation of mind (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is the antidote.
Because both the subject (the mind) and the object (the states to be ceased) would coexist, the definition of the absorption of the cessation of mind would not be established.
As the root treatise says: "Because it must necessarily exist when the three [factors] are in conjunction, and because it possesses efficacy with respect to other absorptions."
If it is claimed that there is mind in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
then since mind arises from objects,
and since the three factors must necessarily come together, there must necessarily be contact (*sparśa*).
Whenever there is contact, it necessarily gives rise to functions such as perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā), just as these functions exist within the four dhyānas.
The Commentary states: "If one accepts the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), there is no fault of contact being absent in this meditative absorption."
If one believes that in the meditative absorption of the cessation of mind there is no other mind but the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
because its subtle and indistinct object is different [from the objects of the active consciousnesses],
then there will be no faults such as the arising of contact and so forth.
If a distinct wholesome mind were to arise apart from the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
this mind would certainly not be separated from the sense organs and their objects.
The conjunction of these three factors necessarily does not occur without contact (sparśa).
The Commentary says: "That which arises from concentration as its cause is characterized by tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).
Tranquility is the characteristic of contact (*sparśa*).
For example, when a person carries a heavy burden, the mind is not tranquil.
If one removes this burden, the body becomes light and the mind is at ease;
this physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is itself contact (*sparśa*),
which is termed *praśrabdhi*.
It is designated as "pliancy" (praśrabdhi).
Because of this transformation into a state of peaceful contact, there necessarily arise the mental factors of pleasant sensation and equanimity.
Subsequently, the name "sensation" (vedanā) emerges, which can be observed.
The Commentary states:
"As for why [this is asked]," this follows upon the preceding statement with the intent of explaining the subsequent seventh fault;
it serves as the reason by which the following text is introduced.

The commentary states: "If it is believed that because there is contact (*sparśa*), this meditative absorption necessarily possesses feeling (*vedanā*), then the claim that 'this state is merely without perception (*saṃjñā*)' is incorrect;
for wherever there is contact, there must necessarily be feeling."
Thus, this meditative absorption cannot extinguish sensation;
it can only suspend perception.
Subsequently, he cites scriptural evidence to show that this statement is incorrect.

The Commentary states: "This contact should not exist [independently], because when contact arises as concomitant and associated with other consciousnesses, there would be the fault that mental attention (*manasikāra*), faith (*śraddhā*), and other roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) would also arise."
The claim that contact exists within this meditative absorption is also untenable; for,
apart from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna),
this contact must necessarily be associated with and co-existent with one of the [six] consciousnesses in the sphere of consciousness.
If it is said that contact exists, then the five wholesome faculties such as faith, as well as mental factors such as attention, should all arise simultaneously;
one cannot say that some exist while others do not.
There is no sense in which one can attain a state associated with wholesome roots such as faith without the application of mental attention (*amanasikāra*).

The Commentary states: "If you say that because one detests contact, feeling, perception, and so forth within this meditative method, these mental factors are uprooted and there remains only mind without contact and the rest—this is not the case."
This immediately refutes their defense.
As they claim:

"Within the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the meditative absorption of the cessation of mind (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one is only averse to mental factors such as contact, feeling, and perception, but not to the mind itself."
Therefore, when concentration is established, it is only the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that are extinguished, not the mind (*citta*).
Since feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) belong to the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), and these universal factors are extinguished, [the mind is not extinguished].
The minor universal mental factors (*anuvyāpaka*), such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, are also extinguished.
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika school explains this meaning as follows:

just as within the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the three dhyānas, one perceives the defects of the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*); therefore, when the three dhyānas are about to arise, the feeling of joy is extinguished, but the mind itself is not extinguished.
In the four dhyānas, the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) is extinguished, yet the mind (*citta*) is not extinguished.
How could one possibly hear it said that the extinction of feeling necessarily causes the mind to be extinguished as well?
The *Śāstra* explains: "Because they are drawn along by these characteristics."
The mind induces mental factors as its own activity;
this "own activity" is precisely the functional capacity of the mind.
Mental factors induce the mind to serve as their support.
Therefore, the mind and mental factors are necessarily inseparable.
The *Vyākhyā* states: "Thus, the mind should be established as being associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment.
This establishes the meaning of mutual induction and inseparability.
If this meaning were established, it would be associated with all mental factors (*caitasika*).
The Commentary states: "If you say that concentration (*samādhi*) and the means to concentration necessarily arise in contradiction with the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*)."
Furthermore, he presents the defense offered by the opponent:
that since this meditative absorption is incompatible with feeling, perception, and mental factors,
and all wholesome roots are associated with the mind, [this absorption must be without them].
Furthermore, since these are mental factors belonging to the categories of feeling and perception, they are all contradicted by this meditative absorption.
Since feeling and perception are extinguished, the roots of goodness are also extinguished.
The Commentary states: "This principle has never been seen elsewhere."
In all the scriptural teachings and the explanations found in the various sections [of the canon],
I have never seen such a meaning;
for how could there be the arising of goodness that is contrary to the roots of goodness?
This principle does not hold.

The *Śāstra* states: "If all phenomena possess a corresponding [condition] because their cause has one, then their similar fruit must also possess a corresponding [condition]; therefore, this position is incorrect."
This meditative absorption takes other superior absorptions as its preliminary means (*upāya*).

Within these preliminary means, it necessarily arises in association and co-arises with various wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), such as feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
Since the cause is associated [with these], it produces a corresponding result, which is the meditative absorption.
The fruit should also be associated with the mental factors.
If one says that the fruit is not associated,
this is also not correct.
The root treatise states,

"Because there is an analogy," which cites the cessation of vitarka and vicāra as necessarily entailing the cessation of speech, and the cessation of the mind as necessarily entailing [the cessation of vitarka and vicāra].
Subsequently, it further presents an external defense of this argument.
He says that just as inhalation and exhalation are bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*),
although these cease in the fourth dhyāna, the body does not perish;
the same applies to the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Although mental formations such as perception are extinguished, the mind itself is not extinguished;
this is also not the case,
because the underlying principles are not equivalent.
The root treatise states: "As it is not the case that all formations are [the same as] all formations.
This means that inhalation and exhalation are not all formations, whereas sensation, perception, and so forth are all formations.
Because inhalation and exhalation do not pervade the three realms;
above the fourth dhyāna, there is no inhalation or exhalation.
Within the desire realm, for example, those born from eggs have no inhalation or exhalation before they emerge from the egg.
Among those born from a womb, from the stage of the *kalala* up to the *ghana*, the bodily parts have not yet developed through their full extent, nor is there inhalation or exhalation.
From the fifth stage, the *praśākhā*, after the nine orifices have opened, inhalation and exhalation then occur.
Because inhalation and exhalation do not pervade [all states], they are said to be "not all formations" (*na sarva-saṃskārāḥ*);
because feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) pervade all three realms and exist everywhere,
they are named "all formations."
Furthermore, mental factors such as sensation and perception are all formations (*saṃskāra*) in relation to the mind;
for it is because these mental factors are present that the mind does not cease.
Initial and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are likewise all formations in relation to speech.
This is because speech necessarily arises from vitarka and vicāra.
Inhalation and exhalation, however, are not bodily formations;
for it is not the case that the body exists only by virtue of these inhalations and exhalations.

The Commentary states: If one were apart from the two breaths of inhalation and exhalation, as well as food, drink, life-span, consciousness, and so forth, these would be able to sustain this body and prevent it from decaying and perishing;
this explains that matter.
Food and drink refer specifically to edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
One does not designate it "food and drink" at the initial moment of ingestion;
rather, it is only when it has been transformed into flavor that it is called food and drink.
From the sequence of flavors, it transforms into the body-element; this is explained as food and drink.
Even when one enters the fourth dhyāna in the lower realms, this body remains sustained by nutriment.
Life-span is itself the fruit;

because the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), in which the ripening of karmic fruits resides, sustains the power and function of this life-faculty (jīvitendriya) throughout this single period of existence, it remains constantly present.
That which prevents this from ceasing is precisely the nutriment of consciousness (vijñānāhāra).
Now, although the bodily formations of inhalation and exhalation have ceased,
this body does not perish because it is sustained by distinct factors such as food, life-force, and the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).
After the mental formations have ceased, what factor sustains the mind so that the mind does not perish?
The Commentary states: "Therefore, this stage" refers to the meditative absorption of the cessation of mind (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Subsequently, it clarifies through two points that the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) exists within this absorption.
First, because the final consciousness arises, one knows that there is a fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Second, because the consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*) sustains the body, one knows that there is a fundamental consciousness.

The Commentary states: "If, from the very beginning, the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*) were to exert such great effort as to uproot the supported and cause it to leave the support, this would not be possible."
The mind is the basis;
mental factors such as sensation and perception are that which depends upon it.
From the very beginning, they are always associated and co-existent, possessing the sense of being inseparable.
Furthermore, there is no great effort capable of causing them to be separated.
The Commentary asks: "Why? Because it is established by way of an analogy.
This refers to an analogy to clarify the point.
The previous citation used "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) as an analogy for "not all conditioned phenomena.
This citation uses the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) as an analogy;
just as there is no causal condition that can cause the four great elements and their derived matter to be separated from one another.
The four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind.
Derived matter consists of the four subtle particles, namely:
visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Since it is impossible to cause them to be separated, the same applies to the mind and its mental factors; they likewise possess no sense of being separable.
Therefore, one cannot extract them individually to make them distinct.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "If it were not the case that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) could be extinguished in this manner, then by mentioning 'all conditioned phenomena' rather than 'some conditioned phenomena,' it would demonstrate the meaning of non-partial eradication.
For example, [factors] such as applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*) are not phenomena that function in all meditative concentrations."
One may attain their cessation according to the depth or shallowness of the meditative concentration.
The *Śāstra* states: "Such cessation is not possible within all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are the dharmas that function within all meditative concentrations."
There is no sense in which this dharma can be separated from the mind such that it would cease.
The Commentary states: "If the universal [factors] were to cease, the mind must necessarily follow them in ceasing.
Universal factors are precisely perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā).
It is also the locus of the omnipresent mental factors. If,
in a mindless absorption, the omnipresent factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) have already ceased,
the mind must necessarily cease along with them.
Subsequently, he cites the Buddha’s words to prove the existence of the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*):
"If the mind and mental factors were to cease and there were no foundational consciousness,
the Buddha would not have said that consciousness does not depart from the body."

Since there is the statement that [the ālayavijñāna] is not separate [from the other consciousnesses], we know that this statement is intended to reveal the existence of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
The Commentary states: "Because there is no fifth indeterminate (avyākṛta) [category]."
Regarding the four types of indeterminate (avyākṛta):
first, that which is produced by good or evil but does not result in [karmic maturation] is the non-obscured indeterminate;
second, the obscured indeterminate.
Just as the afflictions of the upper realms are encompassed and concealed by meditative concentration,
so too is the meaning of the views of self and extremes (satkāya-dṛṣṭi and antagrāha-dṛṣṭi) in the desire realm.
Third, internal and external karmic results, deportment, craftsmanship, transformations, and so forth, are neutral by nature (avyākṛta-svabhāva).
Fourth, that which is obtained through the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of space is entirely truly indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This meditative absorption is necessarily wholesome;
it cannot be either wholesome or unwholesome, nor can it be established as the "unobscured-indeterminate" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) category.
Furthermore, there is no definition of its establishment;
it is a wholesome state acquired through cultivation,
and it is not a karmic fruition.
The practitioners of the Hīnayāna, whose conduct is shallow, do not immediately attain within meditative concentration the deportments, crafts, and transformations;
the Mahāyāna is virtuous in this regard.
For the Hīnayāna, these three all belong to the category of the indeterminate by nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*).
The seeds of the six consciousnesses in a concentrated mind are acquired through cultivation and are not karmic retribution;
karmic retribution refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Furthermore, they do not have the nature of space or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, there is no fifth category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
therefore, it cannot be definitively established as being of an indeterminate nature.

The Commentary states: "Because the three [factors] are capable of bringing about a conjunction, contact gives rise to sensation; if the three lack this capacity for conjunction, then only contact arises and no sensation."
Following the exposition of the meaning of the Hīnayāna, he clarifies that mental factors (*caitta*) are not separate from the mind (*citta*), thereby refuting [the opponent's view].
When the triad of sense organ, object, and consciousness comes together, contact (*sparśa*) necessarily arises;
there is only a difference in whether sensation (*vedanā*) is produced or not produced.
If it were not for the faculties, objects, and consciousness within the preparatory path of the meditative attainment of cessation,
there would necessarily be contact through the conjunction of faculty and object;
from contact, sensation would inevitably arise.
Upon entering the path of skillful means for the cessation of the mind, these three are extremely subtle;
because the functional capacity of the triad of dharmas— perception, non-perception, and consciousness— is weak,
although contact exists, feeling does not arise.
The extremely subtle function takes this as its cause to induce the arising of the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*).
When the concentrated mind arises, there is likewise a conjunction of three factors;
however, because these three factors are so extremely subtle in their conjunction, they no longer possess the capacity to produce feeling (*vedanā*).
Therefore, when sensation is extinguished at this time, it can no longer arise.
Question:
The Mahāyāna clarifies that within the meditative absorption of the extinction of mind (nirodha-samāpatti), there exists the fundamental consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna).
Furthermore, when there is the conjunction of faculty, object, and consciousness, contact must necessarily arise.
Since contact has arisen, does feeling not also occur?
Answer: Yes.
Since there is both extremely subtle touch and extremely subtle sensation,
the *Nirnayācārya-śāstra* (Decisive Treasury Treatise), in its commentary on the "touch" associated with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) among the nine consciousnesses, asks:
"What are the characteristics of the discrimination associated with the fundamental consciousness?"
The fundamental consciousness is always associated with five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-citta-dharma*):
first, volition (*cetanā*);
second, contact (*sparśa*).
Third, feeling;
fourth, perception;
fifth, attention.
These five dharmas, subsumed within their karmic fruition,
are so extremely subtle that even those of great worldly intelligence cannot perceive them;
they arise together constantly and share a single objective sphere.
This fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) experiences exclusively that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), neither suffering nor pleasure.

The nature of the experience is like that of the fundamental consciousness; the experience of the nature of the fundamental consciousness, as well as the experience of the phenomena of the consciousness, are likewise so.
The wording of that treatise is as follows:
"Volition has discernment as its function;
that is to say, it apprehends objects as being either erroneous or correct."
Attention has the function of setting [the mind] in motion;
attention is like the horse's gait,
while volition is like the rider who controls it to go east or west.
Perception (saṃjñā) takes the grasping of objects as its function.
Feeling (vedanā) is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) because it is not defined as either suffering or pleasure;
however, this is not what is being discussed here.
The use of [the term] "□" indicates that the true meaning is different.
The root treatise states: "If there is someone who clings to the view that matter and mind arise in succession," which specifically refutes this divergent attachment.
Because they do not understand that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) serves as the seed,
they claim that form and mind themselves are the seeds of form and mind.
It is precisely to reveal the existence of the fundamental consciousness that the following passage was composed.
This can be seen.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "The aforementioned fault is that if the continuity of consciousness were severed, there would be no cause for subsequent consciousness, and thus it could not arise—as is the case when entering the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth."
"When consciousness has been extinguished and its continuity severed, from what would the subsequent consciousness arise?
The Commentary states: "There are those who hold such a view."
The root treatise refutes only the position that once [the seeds] are severed, there can be no subsequent arising due to the absence of seeds;
it does not refute the principle that matter (rūpa) may arise from the absence of seeds after being severed.
This sentence in the commentary first provides a general indication that [the opponent] maintains that prior matter gives rise to subsequent matter.
Since that [position] is nonetheless refuted, it is said that there are those who hold such a view.

The root treatise states: "As for the specific fault: if a person does not fall back from the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and emerges from the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), then the position held here is untenable."

If this were a fault, it would not mean that the treatise, having already clarified the preceding faults, is now manifesting this meaning; rather, the treatise’s original heading identifies this as a distinct error.
That "this very matter" was mentioned by the author of the treatise is merely to introduce the subsequent distinct errors.
The Commentary says: If it were necessarily so, there would be a specific fault arising from below.
This clarifies that if, as in this case, the continuity were severed and the subsequent mind were to arise again.
This is not a separate error.
It is because the Master of the Treatise first indicated the preceding intention and subsequently gave rise to this specific [point] that this phrase exists.
The Commentary explains: "Because the subsequent mind acts as a cause and is not yet exhausted."
This specifically points out a distinct error:
if there were no fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), then form and mind would not arise from a distinct cause;
rather, preceding form and mind would directly serve as the cause capable of producing subsequent form and mind.
It is said that even after being interrupted during the process of conjunction, [the stream] can arise again later.
If that were so, then when an Arhat enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the final matter and mind would serve as the cause for the further arising of future matter and mind.
In this way, their mutual production is inexhaustible.
As for the statement in the treatise, "If one were to depart from the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*),
this [notion of] grasping would not be established," it refers to the tenets held by schools such as the Saṃmitīya.
The arising of a subsequent form from a preceding form is also termed a "successive condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
the Master of the Treatise now grants that it functions as a successive condition,
yet he does not grant that the mutual production of form and mind constitutes a "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
If it were not for distinct seeds acting as causes and conditions, and if matter and mind were to arise spontaneously, then subsequent matter and mind would likewise arise through their own power;
in that case, matter and mind would produce one another endlessly, resulting in the loss of liberation.
If one were to descend from the state of mindlessness to the realm of birth, there would be no causes or conditions;
thus, it would be impossible for rebirth to occur again.
Such is the logical flaw [in that position].
The third section clarifies that the three meanings [of transformation] would not be established in the absence of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna); this can be seen in the text.

The Commentary states: "If a person were to abide only in the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) and not in the fundamental consciousness, then the meaning of the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) would not be established."
The second section below concerns the realization of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
While both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna clarify the transformation of the basis,
the Hīnayāna explains this transformation in terms of the six consciousnesses.
This meaning is not established.
Only when the Mahāyāna explains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) in terms of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is this meaning established.
Therefore, it is known that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) definitely exists as the basis of reality.
This treatise establishes this through three verses, and the commentary further restates these verses and provides its own explanation.
Within this, there are two sections: the verses and the prose commentary.
There are three points [in this passage].

First, the first two lines and three characters clarify that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) serves as the "causal condition for realization" (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*) of the fundamental transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Second, it clarifies the essential nature and characteristics of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as the locus of the fundamental transformation.
Third, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is refuted because the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) regarding consciousness cannot be established.
To clarify that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) serves as the efficient cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*), the Commentary states:
"That which is free from the five types of distraction."
The five consciousnesses are by nature distracted;
they are naturally incompatible with the outflow-free wisdom of cultivation.
Therefore, this wholesome consciousness is distinct from the other five consciousnesses.
Furthermore, this meaning is free from six kinds of conceptual distraction (*vikṣepa*), namely:
the coarse mental deliberations regarding intrinsic nature, the external, and the internal characteristics, and so forth.
The full significance of this has been explained as previously stated.

The *Śāstra* says: "How is it that they arise in separation at all times? Because such [uncontaminated] arising occurs. This means that in the uncontaminated observing mind, the five consciousnesses do not exist;
it is only upon emerging from meditative observation that the five consciousnesses arise.
Therefore, it is said that "at all times, such [a mind] arises.
The Commentary explains: "Apart from the defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the wholesome consciousness associated with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-vijñāna*).
This explains the meaning of the verse regarding the absence of any other mind.
It is not only free from defiled fivefold sensory consciousnesses,
but also free from defiled mental consciousness and from wholesome mental consciousness associated with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-manovijñāna*).
If one were to speak only of wholesome consciousness without mentioning the remaining states of mind, [the definition would be incomplete].
Thus, there may be a contaminated wholesome mental consciousness included therein.
Now, it is stated that the remaining great minds are known to exist only in uncontaminated wholesome consciousness, which is definitively free from contaminated wholesome [consciousness].

The Commentary states: "Because all seeds of defilement and turbidity have been extinguished, only the fundamental consciousness remains; this is called the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
From here below is the second section, which correctly elucidates the essence of the transformation of the basis.
This passage explains the verse’s question regarding by what means the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is effected.
It sets forth both the essence of the transformation of the basis and the path of the means for that transformation.
Formerly, the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) was mutually supported with the seeds of afflictions and karma.
Now, through the attainment of the untainted path of antidotes, there is liberation;
the seed-consciousness (bīja-ālayavijñāna) undergoes a fundamental transformation (āśrayaparāvṛtti),
whereby the dharma-body becomes the enjoyment-body (sambhogakāya).
Therefore, it is said that there is a "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The phrase "skillful means acts as a finger" is explained later.

The *Śāstra* says: "If you argue that because the antidote arises, the basis is transformed, and thus the path of the antidote is called the 'transformation of the basis,' this interpretation is incorrect."
Regarding this verse, some offer an alternative interpretation:

"If the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa*) constitutes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because the outflow-free path (*anāsravamārga*) arises and the support is transformed from what it was before, then the counteractive path is the essence of the transformation of the basis. This interpretation is not correct.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "The two meanings of not taking cessation (*nirodha*) as the basis of transformation (*āśraya-parivṛtti*) are not established.
This explains the verse by stating that it is "not established because it is not cessation.
These words refute alternative interpretations and set forth the correct meaning.
It is precisely because cessation (*nirodha*) constitutes the essence of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
If cessation were not taken as the transformation of the basis, there would be two faults:
first, even if the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) arises, the seeds of afflictions and karma would not be extinguished.

If there were no seeds within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and only the six consciousnesses existed, then when the supramundane path arises, mundane minds and afflictions would already be absent; what, then, would there be to be extinguished?
[The opponent] says that while [the manifest states] cease, the seeds are not extinguished.
Regarding the second point, that the antidote is the revealing cause of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*):
when the path of the antidote arises, the six worldly consciousnesses are extinguished.
If there were no fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there would be no seeds to be extinguished.
This is because it extinguishes the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
and because the fundamental consciousness transforms into reliance upon the dharma-body; thus,
the path of cultivation is the revealing cause.
It is precisely by taking the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as the substance of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
By specifically eliminating the seeds of evil, the fundamental consciousness attains liberation and realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Based on this Dharma-body, which differs from its previous state, it serves as the transformation of the basis in relation to the dharmas of birth-and-death. This is precisely the cessation of all unwholesome dharmas, the realization of non-arising, and the transformation into the fruit of eternal virtue.
This refers to the meaning of "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti).

The Commentary states: "The transformation of the basis is liberation and the Dharma-body; since these are the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya), one should take the extinction of the seeds as the transformation of the basis."
Herein, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is explained according to its final state.
It clarifies that whereas the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) previously existed as the support for and maintenance of defiled seeds, thereby abiding within saṃsāra,
it has now been purified as the fundamental consciousness is eliminated by the path of remedy.
That is, the body of liberation becomes one with the Tathāgatagarbha;
the Tathāgatagarbha attains the name of the Dharmakāya, and liberation becomes the body of the Saṃbhogakāya.
All path-attainments, merits, and wisdoms follow along with this fundamental essence and transform into manifold virtues.
Because one gives rise to the path of untainted mental consciousness and realizes that the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are empty, it is called "the extinction of delusions.
Since delusions are extinguished, the basis is transformed and one realizes the *dharmakāya*.
If only the path of the six consciousnesses arises,
the mundane mind perishes first,
and the seeds of evil perish along with that mind.
When the Path arises, afflictions and the mind that serves as their basis already no longer exist.
What, then, would the Path sever, what would it extinguish, and what would it transform?
Therefore, one knows that the meaning of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) can only be established if the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) definitely exists.
The Commentary states: If you maintain that when the antidote arises, the seeds of defilement are extinguished, the following refutes that position.
That [position] asserts that the seeds of the antidote are extinguished at one and the same time.
Why is it that cessation is taught but the path is not?
To refute this attachment is now addressed as an error:
the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is the truth of cessation; it is the fruit.
The antidote is the cause;
the cause is the truth of the path;
the path is the revealing cause for the transformation of the basis.
Through the transformation of the basis by means of the cause, cause and effect become non-distinct and form a single entity;
the arising of the path of antidotes is itself parinirvāṇa.
How could such a principle exist? It would then lose the meaning of cause and effect.
The Commentary states: "If there were someone who established the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*)," and so forth.
This is the second section, which correctly refutes the divergent attachments of non-Buddhist schools.
Although both [systems] equally take cessation as the basis of transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*),
they do not establish the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) with respect to the arising of the six consciousnesses.

This refers to the seeds of afflictions and karma produced by the defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which take the mental consciousness as their support (*āśraya*) and the seeds themselves as that which is supported (*āśrita*).
These are extinguished by the path of antidotes (*pratipakṣamārga*).
This relationship between the supported and the support is called the "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
This consciousness does not constitute such a transformation,
because it is only when the mundane mental consciousness has ceased that the knowledge of the path can arise.
When the Path arises, since the two factors—the seed and its support, the mental consciousness—have long been non-existent, what could possibly undergo transformation?
Therefore, the verse says: "Since both are non-existent, the meaning of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is not established."

The Commentary says: Regarding the sixth, the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), if it is not present within the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-avasthā*), there would be no seeds; since there would be neither the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) nor [the evolving consciousness] itself, the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) would not be established.
It is clarified that the Bodhisattva’s stage of non-retrogression is established within the true contemplation of the outflow-free (anāsrava);
at the time when the mind is free from defilement, the defiled consciousness and its seeds have long since naturally ceased and perished.
There are no longer the two factors of worldly mind and seeds;
since these have long been absent, what further could there be to transform?

Because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the Path exist simultaneously, the seeds within the consciousness are eliminated, and the fundamental consciousness undergoes a transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), flowing forth as the Dharma-body.
Thus, the meaning of this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is established.
Therefore, the Commentary states:
"Where there is no seed, there is neither non-action nor non-existence."
First, it is stated that [the agent] does not exist because there is no seed;
subsequently, it is stated that even the mind capable of acting as a seed does not exist, and thus it is said that "non-action" also does not exist.
Chapter Four: On Distinctions. The preceding three chapters have established that the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) exists.
This chapter elucidates the meaning of the various distinct characteristics and functions within the essence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Within this chapter, there are generally two sections;
when further subdivided, they comprise seven sections in total.
The preceding three chapters clarify the meaning of how the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) establishes seeds as its essential nature;

the subsequent chapter is divided into four sections to clarify the fact that the functions of seeds within the fundamental consciousness give rise to the various characteristics and categories of the six destinies, which do not arise through external causes.
Regarding the differences among these first three chapters:
the first generally clarifies the causes of habituation and retribution—
the seeds of all the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of birth and death.
The second clarifies the view of self,
which is the afflictive habituation within the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
The third clarifies the habituation of karma, which has the sense of being the cause for retributive results.
These seven chapters shall be understood according to the explanation in the "Superior Characteristics" (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa) section that follows.
These seven chapters constitute seven sections;
the first chapter is divided into two parts.
The preceding section generally clarified the meaning and intent of the distinctions and combinations within this single chapter.
Second is the formal explanation of the meaning of the first chapter,
which consists of three parts.
First, the listing of the chapter headings;
second, the conclusion summarizing the meaning and intent of the "Question Chapter";
third, the response, which is further divided into two parts.
First, the greatness of the seven intentions is clarified;
second, the names of the three intentions are listed.
This general meaning is evident.

The *Śāstra* states that verbal expression takes as its essence the meaning of the causes of habitual retribution through names; there are two kinds of names, namely, the name of verbal expression and the name of mental reflection. These two kinds of names have sound as their basis.
The following is a brief explanation of the first chapter on verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).
If one understands verbal expression according to its objective basis (*vastu*),
it shares with the name (*nāman*) the same essence, which is sound (*ghoṣa*).
How is this known to be so?
The Sage, for the sake of sentient beings dwelling in the world, reveals that all things have distinctions;
by means of diverse sounds, he establishes the names of all things.
Having repeatedly practiced these sounds, sentient beings grasp at the myriad things as being definitively existent, yet they differ [in their modes of apprehension].
When one opens the mouth and utters sound, it is called "speech" (*vyavahāra*).
When one does not utter speech but directly directs the mind toward contemplation, thinking of the distinct differences among the myriad things, it is called "reflection" (*cintā*).
Although there are these two names, the "Root Chapter" (Mūlapaṭala) is sound;
both take sound as their essential nature.
This is how it should be understood according to the Mahāyāna interpretation of the meaning.
All phenomena have no intrinsic substance; they exist only as verbal designations.
Through repeated habituation, one regards the faculties and their objects as existent, yet this is merely a conventional expression.
Because there is no substantial reality in the myriad things, the perfuming of verbal expression is established as the universal seed for the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of birth and death.
As for "conceptual proliferation," it refers to all that does not take the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as its object; thus, it constitutes the conceptual proliferation of birth and death.

Because these portions of wind-energy perfuse the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and are able to produce the fruits of conceptual proliferation at a later time—specifically, because they generate the functional power of continuity—they are called "seeds" (*bīja*).
The Commentary states: "Regarding the sense organ capable of seeing form, it is spoken of by way of its name, 'the eye.'"
Just as the material sense-faculties can give rise to consciousness that perceives forms,
the name "eye" is established based on this meaning;
the name "eye" is itself a conventional designation.
This is explained according to the principle that there are merely verbal expressions, but no substantial entity.
The Commentary states: "By repeatedly practicing these verbal expressions, one generates an affectionate perfuming within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*)."
Ordinary worldlings habitually practice with this designation;
subsequently, they no longer realize that this name is merely a conventional expression,
and instead cling to the notion that the eye is a distinct entity.
Within that [consciousness], craving arises and repeatedly perfumes the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) with its objects of attachment.
This perfuming possesses a functional capacity that serves as a seed within the fundamental consciousness,
capable of producing the eye in the future.
The same applies to all other phenomena, such as the remaining faculties, objects, and consciousnesses;
this is what is called the "perfuming of verbal expression.

The Commentary states: "There is a defiled consciousness which, by means of the view of self and so forth, arises based upon the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) and perfumes it with notions of 'I' and 'mine'."
Below this is a brief explanation of the second chapter, "The Habitual Impression of the View of Self.
The view of self arises from the *ādāna-vijñāna*’s grasping of the *ālaya-vijñāna* as a self, thereby establishing the distinction between self and others.
Because of this, the six defiled consciousnesses also give rise to the grasping of a self.
The defilement is the ādāna-vijñāna;
the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is that which is defiled.
Following the six consciousnesses, the view of self arises based upon the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), two cognitions arise—the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the view of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*).
These, in turn, perfuse the fundamental consciousness.
Because the fundamental consciousness possesses these seeds, one obtains the retribution of distinct bodies for oneself and others.

The Commentary states: "Because of this perfuming, conceptualization arises—namely, taking oneself as 'self' and that which is other than oneself as 'other'—due to the seeds of the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) existing within the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna)."
At a later time, through this functional capacity, various conceptual discriminations arise that grasp at the existence of these and those realms;
because of this, various afflictions arise,
which in turn perfuse the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to produce various seeds.
This refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and its resultant flow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
The Commentary states: "Regarding the differences in the six sense faculties experienced within the six realms of existence according to wholesome, unwholesome, or immovable karma."
Below this is a brief explanation of the third chapter, "The Habitual Impression of the Existential Portion.
Seeds are termed "existential portions" (*bhavāṅga*).
Karma consists of three grades.
That is to say, there are wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable [karmas].
Wholesome karma brings about rebirth among humans and devas in the desire realm;
unwholesome karma brings about rebirth in the four miserable destinies.
Immovable karma brings about retribution in the two upper realms.
Because "existence" (bhava) refers to that which can obtain the retribution of existence within the three realms and six destinies, it is called "partaking of existence" (bhavāṅga).
The retribution of the three realms and six destinies is precisely the substance of existence.
Due to the activity of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) undergoes transformation through three distinct modes.

By means of these three types of karmic seeds, it is able to transform the fundamental consciousness, giving rise to the various phenomena of suffering and pleasure within the three realms and six destinies.
Afflictions merely have the capacity to induce existence (*bhava*);
they cannot cause the acquisition of various distinct retributions such as suffering or pleasure.
This is precisely because existence arises from karma.
This karma draws forth the various distinctions of existence (*bhava*).
These three chapters constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*);
the first chapter generally concerns the causes of habituation and retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
The second is affliction;
the third is karma.
Thus, there are three distinct chapters.
The root treatise states: "Regarding the differentiation of production.
This explains the fourth chapter, "On Production.
This fourth chapter is explained by the root treatise itself.
The *Śāstra* further explains that there are two types of "projecting": first,
the projecting [cause] which draws forth the seeds that serve as the support for the arising of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), thereby enabling them to be established.
Within the two types of consciousness, seeds draw forth subsequent retributive fruits;
because this chapter elucidates the functional power of such drawing forth, it is called the "Chapter on Drawing Forth.
The root treatise states: "This refers to that which is newly produced through perfuming."
In general, since the past, ignorance and volitional formations have arisen and perfumed the fundamental consciousness;
according to their respective karmas and other factors, those that still possess power and have not yet been experienced all become newly produced.
This is because those who have already obtained the retribution of experience are all considered "old" [beings].

The main treatise states: "If these conditions do not exist, then the principle that 'conditioned by volitional formations (saṃskāra) arises consciousness (vijñāna),' and 'conditioned by grasping (upādāna) arises existence (bhava),' would not be established."
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the past seeds that give rise to the present link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This link of consciousness is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
As the seeds of karma within the fundamental consciousness are about to mature, it brings forth the arising of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Taking these seeds as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) as the causal condition,
it arises by taking the fundamental consciousness as its root.
Regarding "conditioned by grasping, existence arises":
grasping is affliction;
existence is karma.
If there were no fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) acting as the predominant condition,
the seeds would lack a basis for their generative power and efficacy; furthermore,
the mind that performs an action and the mind capable of performing it would cease simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said that this meaning is not established.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Regarding the differentiation of the types of production, this may be understood by referring to each preceding point."
Through repeated cultivation in accordance with the faculties, sense objects, and so forth, seeds are formed;

these in turn produce the results of uniform outflow (niṣyanda-phala) corresponding to what was previously practiced. Depending on whether these results are slight or heavy, one obtains the retributive fruits (vipāka-phala) of pleasure or suffering.
Because there are differences in these retributive fruits, they are said to be distinguished by their "species" (jāti-viśeṣa).
The Commentary says: What is the characteristic of this newly produced perfuming?
Its characteristic is precisely that which produces its own kind by means of newly produced perfuming.

Although it lacks a distinct nature and is likewise indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not devoid of the characteristics of the power and function of the distinctions in its former kinds; thus, it is able to produce the retributive fruits of similar types from previous times.
Therefore, it is said that [the ālayavijñāna] "induces" (ākṣepa). The Commentary states:

"If there were no differentiation within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) that induces, then because the seeds within the fundamental consciousness are capable of inducing subsequent similar fruits, the fundamental consciousness is termed 'inducing'."
As in the past, one receives retribution according to the lightness or heaviness of the karma created and the afflictions involved.

The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding consciousness that is perfumed by conditioned arising and cessation," this clarifies that if conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) were permanent, they would lack the capacity for perfuming.
Because this [consciousness] flows constantly through the arising and ceasing of impermanence, it possesses the meaning of being "perfumed.
That consciousness which is perfumed by those formations (*saṃskāra*) is precisely what draws forth the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
This statement explains the preceding phrase.
The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "because they are comprised by grasping" in relation to that which arises, there are two interpretations.
The first says:
The present appropriation arises by virtue of the power of seeds perfumed by ignorance and formations, based upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);
therefore, the fundamental consciousness is said to be "appropriated" because it serves as the basis for its production.
Because the present bhavāṅga arises in dependence upon the preceding similar cause,
it is said that "arising occurs in dependence on birth.
This is the second point.
Grasping is taken as the cause;
since grasping can induce the arising of existence,
it is therefore called "subsumed under grasping."
It draws forth the existence (bhava) that constitutes the basis for the conditions of future birth;
therefore, it is said to "confront" (abhimukha) birth-existence (upapatti-bhava).
This is precisely the function of ādāna-vijñāna.
The Commentary states: "This existence cannot be established" means that if the seed-consciousness did not exist,
future existence (*bhava*) and so forth would all fail to be established.
This is because there is no dharma that can serve as the causal seed.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Because arising occurs from this, it is said that this is a 'dharma that exists'.
This explains the meaning of "existence" (*sat*).
Because karma performed in the present can bring about the existence (*bhava*) that constitutes the factors for future birth, present karma is therefore called "existence.
The Commentary states: "Grasping (*upādāna*), as well as wholesome and unwholesome [karma], are the fruits of habitual practice from previous lives."

It is explained that because these present appropriations (*upādāna*) and existences (*bhava*) are themselves the wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable karmas, they are said to be the fruits of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) accumulated in past lives.
This means they are produced from the principle of the cause and fruit of that accumulated ignorance.
Liberation from grasping at existence is not of the present.
Grasping has two aspects;
however, it is explained that if there were no projecting cause for the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), [liberation would not occur].
Then, through the seeds perfumed by that practice, the seeds of affliction are correctly eliminated,
whereas the seeds of karma are not correctly eliminated;
once the afflictions have been severed, [the process continues].
The seeds of karma are thereby extinguished.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because what is seen after attaining the Path is pure and differs from what was previously seen, it is said that there is also 'functioning' (*prayoga*)."
After attaining the Way, when one perceives the transformations of others as dust,
one realizes that the essence of this dust is not existent; it is precisely this that is purity,
and it is also the very function of the Way.
Furthermore, the previous explanation states:
after attaining the Way, consciousness does not undergo transformation;
the objects perceived as they originally were are themselves pure.
This is because the seeds of the transforming fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) have already been extinguished;
this is precisely the efficacy of the Path.
The Commentary states: "Because it is maintained by the conceptualization of others."
Because numerous consciousnesses undergo transformation to constitute this objective sphere,
although one's own consciousness no longer undergoes transformation to constitute that original object,
the consciousnesses of others who have not yet attained non-conceptual wisdom still undergo transformation to constitute this objective sphere.
Because this person’s consciousness is sustained by discernment (*vikalpa*), there still remain defiled objects;
this can be understood from the verbal expression.

The *Śāstra* states: "If one extensively generates discernment based on compassion, loving-kindness, and *prajñā*, then because this discernment relies upon *tathatā* (suchness), that which is discerned becomes a pure land."
The Buddha possesses great compassion and prajñā.
By the power of his original vows, he perceives that the conventional is merely consciousness and lacks external objects;
yet, when he perceives the ultimate, although he exercises compassion, he does not differentiate conventional objects.

Because it relies on the wisdom of suchness and is encompassed by prajñā, although it takes conventional objects as its domain, it is free from the conceptualization of those objects as real; through the purity of vision, it is able to manifest a pure land.
In the Pure Land, the wisdom of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) constitutes the essence of the land.
If categorized in terms of ordinary beings and sages, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the truths (*satya*) are all true pure lands.
If categorized in terms of the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), those from the fourth stage upward constitute the true pure land.
Whether through effort or without effort,
the eighth stage is the truly pure land.
Generally, all truly pure lands are lands manifested as the response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
□ From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, these are all true pure lands (*viśuddha-kṣetra*).
Prior to the stages, they are pure lands of marks (*nimitta-viśuddha-kṣetra*);
during the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), they are pure lands of phenomena (*vastu-viśuddha-kṣetra*).
The lands of Maitreya and others are pure by way of their objective reality (*vastu-viśuddhi*);
because those such as the śrāvakas have not yet attained equanimity,
they still discourse on purity by way of objective distinctions (*viśeṣa-viśuddhi*).
Ordinary beings of inferior capacity perceive an impure land and see the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), yet even this does not possess the complete marks.
Those who come from the pure lands of marks belong to the category of the transformation body.
