Bodhisattvas, through the partial severance of ignorance, perceive the pure land; subsequently, having realized the suchness of the three non-natures, they perceive the true pure land.
Ordinary beings perceive an impure land due to the conceptual discrimination of their own minds.
The *Śāstra* asks: "How can it be that a single objective realm is perceived differently by sentient beings?
It is indeed possible for there to be different objects and different perceptions.
Since it is the same single object, why do they each see it differently?

The root treatise states: "For example, when a practitioner of meditation contemplates a single type of object, through various aspirations and various observations, it is established according to the mind."
This is like answering a question:
just as one might take a single object and, through the supernormal powers of a practitioner of meditation,
transform it into various things according to the inclinations and preferences of sentient beings before them.
Regarding "seeing blue and yellow and obtaining auspiciousness":
this refers to the practitioner of visualization observing a single object and unifying it with the color blue;
from small to large, and from narrow to broad, everything becomes the color blue.
It causes the person before one to see blue without giving rise to affliction,
as explained in the "Contemplation of the Ten Bases" (Daśāyatanavipaśyanā).
If these distinct objects were substantially existent, [this would not occur].
Thus, one does not follow the observing mind so as to cause it to become otherwise;
for, being devoid of substantial reality and existing merely as a product of conceptual construction,
one attains the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*) to transform that mind so that what is perceived appears differently to each.
The verse in the root treatise states, "difficult to extinguish and difficult to unravel.
Below this, the second section further clarifies the characteristics of the fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*).
This consists of two parts: a prose commentary (*gadya*) and a verse (*śloka*).
First, that which is to be abandoned is brought forth;
subsequently, the path that serves as its antidote is brought forth.
Regarding the analytical classification of afflictions, there are two types.
This refers to the shared and the unshared.
That which arises resembling external objects is the shared;
that which arises conditioned by internal consciousness is the unshared.
The fetters shared [with other realms] are difficult to eliminate;
the fetters not shared [with other realms] are easy to eliminate.
The general meaning is as explained in the *Śāstra*.
The binding of signs is precisely the conceptual grasping of signs;
that is, [the view] that all external objects perceived by the six consciousnesses exist.
This is because one has not yet realized that these are all produced by the conceptualization of one's own mind.
If one perceives that all signs are produced by the discrimination of consciousness, then desire, hatred, and so forth would have no basis from which to arise.
Furthermore, this is discussed in terms of the two paths: the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation.
Because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is difficult to obtain,
the attainment of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) occurs through the elimination of afflictions by means of the path of uninterrupted transition;
once the afflictions have been extinguished, the path of liberation arises spontaneously immediately thereafter.
This refers to the difficulty of attaining the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The root treatise states: "The minds of those practicing contemplation differ due to the great magnitude of external characteristics.
The commentary explains that this is difficult to understand and difficult to extinguish for three reasons.
First, because external phenomena do not exist, one contemplates only the internal treatment.
Second, because its characteristics pervade the ten directions, it is called "great.
Third, it clarifies that the contemplation of the mind contradicts internal seeds and has no connection with the external.
Therefore, it is said that external difficulties are hard to extinguish and hard to resolve.
What follows clarifies that when the mind is pure, one sees purity.
Below this, the second section clarifies the path of antidotes, which is further divided into two parts.
First is the primary path that is truly capable;
second, both attain the elevation of the object to establish the practice.
When the path of remediation is fulfilled, this constitutes the purification of the divisions.
When the Path is not yet perfected, one attains purification according to one's respective degree.

Through the clarity of the Dharma, one perceives the true reality (*tathatā*) and the characteristics of phenomena; with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), one penetrates and sees both the ultimate and conventional truths as empty.
Subsequently, through subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one perceives that the conventional consists only of consciousness, which is a false existence.
All other phenomena are entirely empty and non-existent;
sentient beings are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), which is the dependent and constitutes the conventional reality of the essence.
The wisdom of mere-consciousness is the basis upon which it depends, serving as the essence of the pure land.

The wisdom that arises from True Suchness (tathatā) regarding the embryonic cycle of birth and death constitutes the true essence, which is precisely the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna).
By relying on this wisdom, one inquires into and advances toward benefiting others and so forth, thereby attaining the fulfillment of the Dharmakāya.
Therefore, it constitutes the substance of the land.
The *Śāstra* asks about the causes and conditions for the manifestation of the original pure land:
"As for seeing the Buddha’s purity..."
Seeing the Buddha is the wisdom of the true essence (*samyag-jñāna*).
Based on this, the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*) arises,
which constitutes the substance of the land.
Because one advances through subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and increases the fivefold factors of the Dharma-body (*pañcadharmaskandha*),
this land has that knowledge as its basis;
therefore, it is the essence of the land.

The Commentary states: "A bodhisattva who cultivates internal contemplation without relying on the external" clarifies the second stage of the practice of contemplation within the process of observation.
It is called "not relying on the external" because the external is merely that which originally exists [as an object].
This reveals the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
The Commentary states: "Second, by this contemplation that there is only consciousness and no external objects.
This means that by contemplating that within there is only consciousness, one reveals the absence of external objects.
This concludes the demonstration of the characteristics [of consciousness].
Hereafter, it clarifies how various people perceive external objects through different perspectives;
by observing how a single object is established according to one's own inclinations and desires, the meaning of "consciousness-only without external objects" becomes evident.
The Commentary says: "If external objects truly existed, the practitioner's aspiration would not be fulfilled; because the cause is not established.
This is because, since there are no objective entities (*artha*), various practitioners may form various aspirations regarding a single object, and these aspirations will be fulfilled accordingly.
This constitutes proof by reason:
if external objects truly existed such that they could not be subverted as in the two types of emptiness,
then the work performed by the practitioner would be rendered ineffective.
This constitutes a failure of the reason (*hetu-asiddha*).
This subsequent passage, as well as the connection between the preceding and following sections, can be understood accordingly.
The root treatise states: "It is the uncommon, fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which possesses the seeds for the arising of sensation and perception through differentiation."
Below this is the explanation of the third section, which provides a detailed analysis to demonstrate its characteristics.
This consists of five parts.
The first clarifies the principle that common and uncommon causes together produce a single fruit.
1. Distinguishing between the characteristics of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and the characteristics of subtle lightness;
2. Clarifying the two types of seeds: those with sensation (*sopādāna*) and those without sensation (*anupādāna*); 3.
Explaining how the seven consciousnesses perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), as well as the mental afflictions (*kleśa*) upon that consciousness.
Regarding the five types of seeds—those with complete fetters, those with incomplete fetters, and those that are seeds—the present text states:
previously, it was explained that non-common seeds arise independently to produce a single fruit;
now, it is shown that when they are assisted by other factors, they are established as the objective realm for other sentient beings.
Therefore, the text says:
"If these sentient beings did not exist, the conditions for the arising of the world would not be established.
These conditions for arising are precisely the auxiliary factors that bring about the formation of those objective realms.
Regarding the conditions for the arising of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*):
it can be understood that the world arises through the primary agency of one lord assisted by other beings.
Furthermore, there are those who assist in the formation of other bodies, bringing about objects of my own attachment and aversion.
Therefore, it is established that the meaning of "dust" (rajas) refers to their being perceived as equal.
The *Vyākhyā* states: "This passage clarifies that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the concordant fruit of both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
This is because, secondly, the fundamental consciousness is perfumed by both wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
The two kinds of seeds within the fundamental consciousness are themselves the concordant fruits.
These retributive seeds undergo transformation as causes to bring about the arising of retribution;
furthermore, performing good or evil acts constitutes the cause.
The Commentary states: "Because the mind lacks functional capacity regarding both principle and phenomena, it is termed 'coarseness and heaviness' (*dausthulya*).
Not comprehending the principles is called 'coarse';
being unable to apply correct diligence is called 'heavy.'"
This refers to the delusions of both the large and small consciousnesses.
"Delusion" is explained as before.
Because these large and small delusions exist, one is distracted and coarse, unable to penetrate the phenomena and their underlying principles; therefore, it is called "coarse."
Furthermore, because the mind becomes sunken and weak due to these afflictions, and lacks the vigor of exertion, they are called "heavy.
The characteristics of "subtle" and "light" are understood by reversing the explanation of the former.

As for why only contaminated wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) are described as subtle and light, while uncontaminated wholesome states (*anāsrava-kuśala*) are not: [it is because the latter are inherently subtle and light].
The present treatise discusses the meaning of the seeds of saṃsāra, the fruits of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*), and the fruits of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wholesome states extinguish the seeds of saṃsāra;
uncontaminated wholesomeness is characterized as a subtle and light consciousness.

The root treatise states: "If, without this [basis], the distinction between the supports that possess superior capacity and those that lack superior capacity resulting from prior karma could not be established, then consciousness possesses two parts:
the coarse and heavy (*dausthulya*) and the subtle and light."
These two parts— the seeds of good and evil produced by prior karma that bring about retribution,
and the further performance of good and evil karma within that retribution—
cannot be established as a coherent or liberating explanation.
The body of the evil realms and so forth, which is induced by the ripening cause of unwholesome [karma] and the like,
is termed "coarse" because its physical form and appearance are ugly;
it is termed "heavy" because it lacks power and capability.
Due to the cause of the retribution of wholesome karma, one receives the superior retribution of the human and celestial realms;
because its form and color are subtle, it is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
Furthermore, because it possesses superior power and efficacy, it is called "light" (*laghu*).
This explains the presence or absence of power based on the retributive form-body (*vipākārūpakāya*).
Furthermore, the fruit of retribution obtained through unwholesome karma is incapable of functioning within this supramundane principle or in the practices to be performed.
The retribution obtained from wholesome karma possesses the power to function regarding supramundane phenomena and principles.
Furthermore, unwholesome karma can produce its own fruit, and that fruit,
in turn, acts as an acquired cause (*vāsanā-hetu*) for the production of subsequent afflictions and unwholesome karma.
Through wholesome karma one is able to obtain its fruit;
that fruit, in turn, acts as a causal condition for the arising of subsequent supramundane wholesome karma, such as the faculties of faith and so forth.
The Commentary states: "If the fundamental consciousness did not possess these two characteristics, the principles of cause and effect would both fail to be established."

That is to say, if the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) did not exist, then the characteristics of cause and effect for both the wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the characteristics of cause and effect for both habituation and retribution, would all be untenable.
This is as previously refuted regarding the fallacy of having no basis.
When this consciousness is established,
the principle of cause and effect is thereby attained.
As was previously stated regarding the distinction of the basis:
It takes the retributive bodies of the six realms as its basis;
it is called "differentiated" because the six realms are distinct from one another.
The root treatise states: "Furthermore, there are two kinds of fundamental consciousness: those with the characteristic of being experienced and those without."
Below this, the second section clarifies the characteristics of not receiving cause and effect.
Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), seeds possess two kinds of functional capacities:
first, the capacity to produce the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
Second is the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
When this cause ripens and the fruit of maturation arises, that seed is then exhausted.
If it produces a fruit of similarity (*niṣyandaphala*), [the seed is not exhausted].
This is inexhaustible,
because the causal conditions of habituation produce fruits without end. Therefore,
it is said that the seeds which induce the fruit of retribution are termed "possessing the characteristic of appropriation."
The seeds that produce results similar [to their cause] are called "not receiving retribution," because they do not receive a fruit of retribution;
this is precisely the meaning of the "cause of habituation" (*vāsanā-hetu*).

The root treatise states: "If this consciousness did not exist, then the principle that good and evil karma—whether performed or not performed—is exhausted through the experience of its fruit of retribution would not be established."
If mental karma and the like did not have the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) to sustain their seeds,
then what was to be performed would fail to yield its fruit,
and what was performed would fail to yield its fruit.
Therefore, it is said that there would be an exhaustion of the fruit;
if the meaning of non-exhaustion cannot be established,
then action would exist without its result being obtained.
The notion that results are obtained without action would have to be established as a mere abbreviation; however,
there is no principle whereby results are obtained spontaneously.
Since there would be no principle for attaining the fruit without [a basis for] non-action,
we know that the fundamental consciousness exists to maintain it so that it is not lost.
The four propositions presented later are merely a distinct interpretation.
However, regarding the karma created by beings of the four modes of birth, there are four permutations of wholesome and unwholesome karma:
there is that which is performed but not accumulated;
and there is that which is accumulated but not performed.
There is that which is both committed and prolonged,
and that which is neither committed nor prolonged.
If one commits an act oneself but regrets it and does not continue it further, this constitutes the first case.
If one does not act oneself but merely rejoices in the actions of others, this refers to the second phrase.
To perform an action and continue to carry it out refers to the third phrase.
The final phrase refers to neither acting nor increasing [the karma].
It can be seen that because one neither creates nor continues any good or evil karma as it arises, [the result does not follow].
Now, only the first two phrases are cited.

Because there is that which can induce a result, there is the sense of exhaustion. Since the first two [categories] are capable of inducing results, and the third is an object of knowledge, it too is capable of inducing them;
the fourth, however, lacks such a cause.
The Commentary states: "Because the seeds of common karma have this continuity as their cause, it is called the characteristic of non-appropriation.
This means that since common karma refers to the sense of the subsequent continuity arising from the habitual causes of a particular type, it is termed the "cause of non-interruption."
Because it is neither painful nor pleasant feeling, it is said to have the characteristic of non-feeling.
This clarifies the divisions.
If these three were manifested as established:
All phenomena exist only as names and expressions;
they are regarded as existent through inverted conceptualization,
for one habituates to these names and expressions as being existent.
Because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is perfumed to form seeds, it is called "naming and conceptualization perfuming" (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*).
These two types of discrimination—between phenomena and principles—are termed the "outer and inner afflictions" (*tvak-māṃsa-kleśa*).
Furthermore, within these phenomena and principles, the differentiation of all meanings within each as various distinct varieties is termed "mental affliction" (*citta-kleśa*).
This refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance.
It clarifies that all seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing do not take real objects as their conditions;
because of beginningless conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there exist seeds of causal habitual tendencies which constitute the characteristic of non-apprehension.
The Commentary states: Because the functional capacity for yielding fruit has been extinguished through giving and one no longer undergoes retribution, it is called "consumption.
If there were no non-consumption, then the fruit of habituation would lack its cause of habituation, resulting in its severance and the absence of continuity.
If there were no seeds characterized by sensation, there would be no fruit of retribution, nor the cause-and-effect relationship of such fruit.

Because these two characteristics of sensation exist, once the fruit of retribution already experienced has been exhausted, and the fruit not yet experienced arises, one undergoes [rebirth]; thus, there is the sense of exhaustion.
Therefore, there is no loss of liberation.

The Commentary states: "Because of the meaning of losing liberation" refers to the fact that because the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) have not yet been exhausted, and because they undergo exhaustion, there is liberation.

The subsequent clarification that the seeds of the unappropriated characteristics are themselves the causal condition for habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*) can be understood from the words of the *Vyākhyā*.
The *Vyākhyā* states: "If there were no afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, then there would be neither existence (*bhava*) nor its differentiation."
"Existence" (bhava) refers to the three realms of existence;
"differentiation" refers to the six destinies.
It is the distinction between the various destinies of the six paths, brought about by karma that induces existence through the power of afflictions.

The Commentary says: For example, just as a magical illusion of elephants, horses, and so forth is the cause for a distracted mind, so too is the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna)—being the seed of false discrimination—the cause for all inverted and distracted minds.
The fourth section provides its own explanation following the various analogies:
the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are the causes and conditions for all the deluded minds of birth-and-death and inversion;
these seeds give rise to all the deluded minds of birth-and-death.
Just as illusory elephants and horses serve as conditions for a distracted mind to give rise to further distraction,
I shall now briefly present four analogies.
These correspond to the four delusions within the *dhātu* (constituent) that give rise to the six consciousnesses and their associated mental perversions.
That which can produce grasping and attachment through illusory phenomena is actually small beans, yet they are now made into an army and horses;
because one grasps them as real soldiers and horses, this is grasping and attachment.
To illustrate that within the cycle of birth and death there is in reality only consciousness— just as with small beans—
one’s mind, inverted by ignorance, perceives the non-existent self and objects, and falsely interprets them as truly existing sixfold objects.
Just as illusory phenomena cause one to perceive elephants and horses,
they thus give rise to grasping and attachment.
Next, regarding the mirage that can produce craving and affection in sentient beings:
Just as a thirsty deer perceives a shimmering mirage in the heat of the sun as water,
and out of craving for that water runs toward it and pursues it, yet never sees it; this serves as an analogy to clarify how,
within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), there is in reality no such thing as craving, yet one clings to its existence and gives rise to craving therein.
Just as there is in fact no water within a mirage, yet one perceives water therein and gives rise to craving;
so too, dream-images can produce the distracted minds of sentient beings.
When one sees the five sense-objects within a dream, all such things give rise to various kinds of distracted minds.
By investigating this through the principle of awakening, one finds that in reality nothing exists; yet it continues to give rise to false views.
This serves as an analogy for how birth and death are like the five sensory objects seen within a dream, such that all desires arise.
When the wisdom of true suchness awakens, there is nothing further to be seen;
only then is it verified that there is merely a distracted mind and no actual objective realm.
The cataract-like obstruction prevents sentient beings from clearly perceiving the realm.

Because of *dāna* (generosity), one is unable to penetrate the principle; because of clinging to the *ālayavijñāna* as a self and so forth, the six consciousnesses are defiled, creating obstacles that prevent penetration of the principle—namely, all principles such as the Truths and the Jewels.
The remainder is entirely as in the *Śāstra-vyākhyā* (Shìlùn) and is easy to see. Next, the meaning of being bound by both [afflictions] and not being bound by both is clarified.
The visible locations have been explained;
for the invisible locations, they are not detailed here, but their reception is briefly indicated.
In the fifth section, if one discusses the two obstacles in relation to the wisdom of liberation:
the Tathāgata extinguishes both obstacles simultaneously,
whereas the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas extinguish only the single obstacle to liberation.
If one discusses this in terms of the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*),

there are two ways of explaining how the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) is common to the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*): [the first] clarifies the meaning by means of the obstacle of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the obstacle of mind (*citta*).
The delusions of view constitute the flesh;
the delusions of cultivation constitute the skin.
According to this principle, while the followers of the Two Vehicles have severed the two obstacles of flesh and skin, they have not yet severed the obstacle of the mind.
If one clarifies the meaning of the future limit of the Mahāyāna,
then the mind is severed at the eighth stage,
and meat is severed from the first stage upward.
Before the stages [of the path of seeing], one abandons the "skin.
According to this principle, the śrāvakas have not yet completely abandoned the skin;
even the ignorance as numerous as the sands of the Ganges belongs to the obstruction of the skin.
The two vehicles only achieve the simultaneous abandonment of delusions at the fifth stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*),
whereas the great practices are able to suppress and abandon the sands-of-the-Ganges-like ignorance (*avidyā*) from the sixth stage upward.

Among these, although the sands-of-the-Ganges-like habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance are suppressed and abandoned during the fifteen stages, they are still unable to sever the essential substance of the delusions themselves.

Upon reaching the final mind of the stage of the seeds of the Path (*mārga-bīja*), one only then subdues and extinguishes [the afflictions], exhausting the outer skin; this is merely a partial explanation. The subsequent clarification of the meaning of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) as the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is as explained previously;
it shall be further explained in detail hereafter.
The subsequent section, "The Chapter on the Non-attainment of All Phenomena in the Absence of the Fundamental Consciousness," clarifies that the fundamental consciousness is neutral (avyākṛta).
Therefore, it is evident that the perfuming of the three natures occurs through craving; this is reiterated later after the discussion on afflictions.
The fruit of retribution is precisely the mind-ground that is neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
When performing good or evil, it does not constitute [a karmic result] because it belongs to the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
(From the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, Fascicle Five)
The Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Seven:
Associating with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) is precisely what gives rise to the power of practice and understanding (*pratipatti-adhimukti-bala*). [Text missing].

It is said that having already entered into resolute faith and joy (*adhimukti*), it is also called the power of correct reflection (*samyak-manasikāra-bala*) and the power of application (*prāyogika-bala*).
The power of practice.
By virtue of the causal power cultivated through immeasurable past lives,
one attains the opportunity to serve the Buddhas as a condition for cultivating the path.
Having encountered a Buddha and heard the Dharma, one gives rise to right reflection and develops resolute faith and delight;
to then diligently cultivate this very Dharma in which one has faith constitutes the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The stage of faith and aspiration (*śraddhā-prasāda*) is indeed universal;
however, the specific locus currently being established pertains to the ten stages of revolving (*daśa-āvartana*), wherein one has faith and aspiration.
This refers to the meaning of the threefold Buddha-nature (*trividha-buddhadhātu*), as explained previously.
The Commentary states: "Not being subverted or destroyed by bad friends and the like" means that the two vehicles are bad friends;
they cannot destroy the bodhisattva’s mind of faith and aspiration.
"Once the mind has been established as unshakable," and so forth;
that is, various skillful means employed by celestial Māras and non-Buddhists cannot cause the Mahāyāna mind to turn back.
The root treatise states: "Because one has well matured, cultivated, and increased the roots of goodness, one thus successfully acquires the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom."
This is the fourth reliance on power.

By virtue of the power of cultivating preparatory application, one attains the maturation of the accumulations of merit and wisdom, becoming fully perfected, and thus enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
This is precisely the reliance of the first stage, which also encompasses its sustaining support.
By means of the provisions (*sambhāra*), one is able to sustain and accomplish the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Upon ascending to the first stage, because the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) has been accomplished, one enters it. As for the statement "well-matured cultivation and growth of the roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*): [This refers to] the fact that through the practice of the provisions, the roots of goodness are brought to full maturity, cultivated, and increased. Thus, by virtue of these matured roots of goodness, one attains entry into the first stage. This is what is meant by "well-matured cultivation and growth of the roots of goodness."
One should skillfully cultivate five meanings:
first, the absence of conceptual differentiation regarding the agent, the object of action, and the purpose of the action;
second, cultivation free from attachment.
This refers to the Temple of Repaying Kindness through Causes and Retribution, which is not attached to causes or retribution.
Third is non-contemplative cultivation,
which means not contemplating the characteristics of cause and effect, the agent and the object of action, or even the aspects of cause and effect and so forth.
Fourth is the cultivation that is free from causing offense.
This means that one’s conduct accords with principle and is personally free from even the slightest fault,
and furthermore, one is able to cause others’ minds to receive benefit according to their individual capacities.
Fifth is the cultivation of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
One employs all various practices to bestow them upon sentient beings;
furthermore, for the sake of the four modes of birth, one dedicates them toward unsurpassed bodhi and, reaching the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), dedicates the fruits back to sentient beings.
Because it possesses these meanings, it is called "well-cultivated.
There are four meanings to the cultivation of maturation:
first, long-term cultivation.
Second, uninterrupted cultivation;
third, respectful cultivation;
fourth, exhaustive cultivation.
To investigate and cause [the qualities] to increase is what is meant by "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
As for the statement in the root treatise, "Therefore, one who has properly acquired the two kinds of provisions— merit and wisdom"—
if this is discussed in terms of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*):
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and meditative concentration constitute merit;
wisdom constitutes insight;
and diligence pertains to both.
Whatever merit is generated through such exertion belongs to the category of merit;
the wisdom resulting from that exertion is subsumed under the category of wisdom.
The root treatise asks: "In what state do the bodhisattvas practice so as to enter the contemplation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*)?"
The third section below clarifies the Chapter on Entering the Elements (*dhātu*).
It correctly elucidates the objective realm of contemplative wisdom;
the subsequent explanation will be evident.
This question has two intentions:
first, it asks about the object;
second, it asks about the stage. In the response, this chapter specifically answers the question regarding the object.
Chapter Four provides the formal response regarding the presentation of the stages.
The Commentary states: "This dharma is called the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-bhāvanā*), and it is also called the 'object' (*viṣaya*).
This means that the contemplation of consciousness-only can sustain this object and cause it to manifest before one.
Furthermore, this object is precisely that which sustains the cultivation of the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
The objective domain of the contemplation of consciousness-only does not transcend these four propositions.
If one does not recognize these four propositions, one will likewise be unable to enter the principle of the contemplation of consciousness-only.
The objects of focus and the realms of perception subsumed within the contemplation of consciousness-only do not transcend these four propositions.
As for "dharmas," there are two types: first, those with visibility;
second, those with characteristics.
That is: first, the manifestation of the semblance of the meaning of dharmas;
second, mental verbalization and discrimination;
third, that which arises from the characteristics of the Mahāyāna dharma.
The previous statement that all perceptions are the activity of the discriminating manovijñāna (mental consciousness),
and that apart from this there is no separate dharma to constitute the two [subject and object],
is explained in the Commentary as follows: "Because the characteristics of the Mahāyāna serve as the cause, [the perception] arises."
To clarify this meaning: the conceptualization of verbal expression is correct reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

Within correct reflection, both the views and the signs arise because they are produced by the prior reception of the Mahāyāna teachings and the resulting perfuming (*vāsanā*); therefore, it is said that they arise with the Mahāyāna dharma-characteristics as their cause.
The Commentary states: "In this context, 'manifesting the object' refers to conceptualization through mental discourse (*manojalpa-vikalpa*).
Because there is no objective realm (*viṣaya*) apart from the conceptualization of vitarka and vicāra, conceptualization through mental discourse constitutes the essence of the object."

The Commentary states: "Regarding the manifestation of the characteristics of the objective sphere, which refers to that which has both seeing and characteristics—what kind of characteristics does the mental verbalization (manojalpa-vikalpa) possess?
This discrimination does not go beyond taking the two factors of characteristic and seeing as its objective sphere."
The subsequent sentence seeks the cause and does not differ from the preceding one.

The *Vyākhyā* states: "Regarding these four stages of the conceptualization of mental discourse (*manojalpa-vikalpa*)," this refers to the fourth chapter, "Entering the Stages," which answers the section on the stages in the third chapter mentioned above.
Question: It is taught that the contemplation of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) has four stages, all of which have mental verbalization (manojalpa-vikalpa) as their essence.
One forms understandings of the principles and phenomena of all dharmas, realizing that everything is the conceptualization of consciousness.
This means that although there are appearances of perceived objects and so forth, in reality there is only a single consciousness.
Nevertheless, although the four stages are all equally entry into the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*),
in truth there are profound differences in their depth.
This chapter consists of four sections:
first, the designation of the stages;
second, the explanation and demonstration of the characteristics of the stages.
The third [section] establishes the characteristics of the stage and its sphere;
the fourth provides a concluding demonstration of its essential nature.
The root treatise states: "Because one enters the stage of the ground of vows and practices (praṇidhānacaryābhūmi) by means of faith and delight according to what has been heard."
In the root treatise, the names of the four positions are first listed, and they are subsequently explained through four meanings.
The commentary fully cites both the preceding and following texts; that is to say, the words are separated first, and only thereafter are they joined for explanation.
The same applies to the four stages.
This is because the text states that one has "faith and delight according to what has been heard.

That is to say, for one who has developed faith and delight regarding the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only) based on what has been heard, the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) has not yet been well-established.
Therefore, the stage prior to the ground (*bhūmi*) represents the position of faith and aspiration (*adhimukti*).
As for the statement in the root treatise, "The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is defined as thorough penetration according to reality," at the stage of faith and aspiration,
the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) has not yet been accomplished.
One immediately enters the first realization of bodhi, wherein the abiding mind and principle become one;
this is non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna),
and it is also true prajñā.
This wisdom has not yet perfected conventional observation;
it is only when one finally perceives that objects are signless (*animitta*) that the observation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is perfected.
That is to say, because the conditions for arising have been exhausted, it is signless.
Because the marks are exhausted, consciousness is non-arising;
the conditions themselves are non-arising.
By these two names, it is the reality.
Since true reality fundamentally lacks the mutual production of characteristics, it further lacks the opposition of mutual production;
thus, it is established as being without intrinsic nature.
This very nature is true *prajñā*.
Relying upon the original vow, [the practice] continues to arise;
only after attaining subsequent wisdom (prajñā) does one clearly perceive the meaning of representation-only (vijñapti-mātra) within the conventional world.
Therefore, this is called "thorough penetration" (prativedha).

The Commentary says: "This conceptualization of mental discourse, which appears as if it possessed characteristics, is thoroughly understood to not exist in that way, but to be mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
This clarifies the vision of the emptiness of the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The appearance manifested by the conceptualization of mental discourse is precisely the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
This is in reality non-existent; it is merely the measure of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), which is the nature of signlessness (*animitta-svabhāva*).
The *Śāstra* states: "This consciousness is neither dharma nor artha, and is neither the grasper nor the grasped.
This clarifies that when one contemplates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), consciousness arises based on its original object; this is what is called "consciousness."
Since the objects of the grasper and the grasped lack any characteristic, consciousness does not possess the nature of a grasper.
Being neither a seeing nor an object, it is also not that which is grasped.
Since it is neither grasper nor grasped, consciousness is without arising.
Because there is no longer any distinction between self and other, or between this and that, it is neither dharma nor meaning, and is detached from suchness (*tathatā*).
Since non-existence is itself suchness, one immediately enters the principle of the three natures of non-nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāva*).
At that time, consciousness is not perceived; there is only this single suchness.
This refers to the meaning of the correct view of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) within the preparatory stages (*pūrvaprayoga*) and the main practice (*maula*).
The Commentary states: "Observing in this manner can counteract all three obstacles.
There are two types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the stage of practice.
One major division:
taking the first stage as the stage of vision (darśana-bhūmi) and the second stage and above as the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-bhūmi).
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward is the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), because the application of effort has reached its consummation.
Second, regarding the subdivisions:
within each stage, there are three phases.
When the entry is complete, it is both the culmination of entry and the emergence from entry;
these three stages also constitute the culmination of the paths of seeing and cultivation.
Regarding the path of cultivation, there is the sense of progressive advancement and the sense of increasing illumination.
Thus, it is able to remedy all obstacles.
Regarding the statement "all three obstacles," this refers to the three: the skin, the flesh, and the heart.
The afflictions, karma, and retribution are also threefold;
liberation, meditative concentration, and wisdom are likewise threefold.
Because such is the case, it is said that there are "all three obstacles."
Furthermore, they may also be categorized as threefold according to the superior, middling, and inferior grades.
The *Śāstra* states: "This path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is not different from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), by virtue of both wisdom (*jñāna*) and its object (*ālambana*).
Although the two paths of seeing and cultivation differ in their depth, [they are not distinct in essence].
Because they equally attain non-conceptual wisdom and equally realize the principle of the three natures of non-existence,
it is said that this meaning is not different.
The commentary briefly indicates the five points of difference in their characteristics.
The first [point] is clear.

Regarding the second, it is said that excluding the obstacles common to the three vehicles is called the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), while excluding only the obstacles specific to Bodhisattvas is called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This is because followers of the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) only sever the afflictions of seeing and cultivation, which are the obstacles to the fruit, but have not severed the obstacles to the cause.
This takes the first category of ignorance as its cause.

As for "being the nature of an ordinary person," it means that the fundamental nature of an ordinary person's delusions is capable of producing the delusions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
This is precisely the root of the afflictions of both the paths of seeing and cultivation.
Now, severing the obstacles of the first stage is itself the severing of the fundamental cause of the three vehicles;
therefore, it is called the "universal obstacle" of the three vehicles.
Regarding what is severed by the three vehicles:
within the ten stages of practice and five minds, the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are completely severed;
from the sixth mind upward, one merely suppresses and severs ignorance.
Ignorance is precisely the root of the afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
On the stages (bhūmi), one abandons the obstacle of the selfhood of phenomena (*dharmātmagraha-āvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, according to certain interpretations, it is taught that the two vehicles also abandon these afflictions.
Because the two truths and their two characteristics still appear with strong conceptual force up through the seventh stage, they are called "the Two Vehicles" (*dvayayāna*).
This does not mean that the Two Vehicles have severed the afflictions of the three realms and abide [in their realization].

Regarding the third explanation, it says: "That which has not yet perfected its contemplation and lacks the possibility of retreating is called the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); that which has not yet perfected its contemplation and possesses the possibility of retreating is called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
The Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) is eternally established as being of one meaning with true reality;
therefore, it is clarified that there is no retrogression from it.

As for the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), because one constantly enters principle through skillful means and repeatedly emerges from the mundane world to progress toward the severance of delusions by means of the practice of Consciousness-Only (vijñapti-mātra), it is said that there is retrogression.
The truths of principle and phenomena, as well as the ultimate and conventional, are always concurrent;
here, one side is taken up for illustration.
The fourth [section] explains that what is called the "path of seeing" (darśanamārga) refers to the contemplation of the common object.
Thus, True Suchness (tathatā) serves as the universal object.
Since the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) takes both the ultimate and conventional meanings as its objects, it is both universal and particular;
whereas the path of seeing (darśanamārga) takes only the meaning of perceiving the principle [of reality].
The *Vyākhyā* on the fifth [chapter] states: "The accomplishment of the task (*kāryasiddhi*) is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Because one attains the state of non-effort (*anābhoga*) through the culmination of effort and application, it is termed 'accomplishment of the task.
The root treatise says: 'Within the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*), it is because one has emerged from obscurations and defilements and is most pure.'"
The eighth stage, the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), is the culmination.
The two types of stages are explained as previously stated.
The commentary says: "Because this stage is the source from which the most pure wisdom arises."
Non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) that functions spontaneously without deliberate mental attention and is itself signless is pure wisdom;
furthermore, the fulfillment of each stage (*bhūmi*) is also pure wisdom.

The Commentary states: "Because the most subtle obstacles are extinguished without remainder" means that, with respect to these respective stages of the Great and Small Vehicles, the afflictions pertaining to each stage are exhausted without remainder.
If one asks what object is taken as the focal point when entering these four stages,
the third section below indicates the objects;
hereafter, with the exception of non-conceptual *tathatā* (suchness), [all other phenomena are included].
Regarding the conventional wisdom perspective, all objects of cognition are nothing but consciousness.
The "four realms" consist of the three realms plus the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), making four in total.
The *Vyākhyā* states: "All phenomena take consciousness as their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and suchness (*tathatā*) as their essence (*svabhāva*)."

From "For what reason? onwards is the fourth section, which, based on conventional truth (*saṃvṭti-satya*), explains that although all phenomena (*dharma*) differ from the ultimate reality, they are nothing but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Thus, by taking consciousness as the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), one realizes the ultimate reality as awakening.
There is only suchness, in which object and cognition are non-different;
outside of this, there is no other dharma.
For anything distinct from suchness is conventionally like an illusion, as it lacks a separate substantial entity.
Being non-different from *tathatā*, it takes *tathatā* itself as its essence.
If one interprets this in the sense of arising in accordance with delusion, it is consciousness (*vijñāna*); when delusion ceases and there is no arising, that is *tathatā*.
Therefore, all phenomena have *tathatā* as their essence.
It does not have anything other than this suchness as its essence.
The Commentary states: "If the path of expedient means takes consciousness as its characteristic, when one enters the path of seeing, it takes suchness as its essence."
On the path of skillful means, one perceives that only consciousness has substantial reality;
apart from consciousness, all things are like dream-objects and do not exist at all.
Consciousness arises because it follows after delusory objects.
Since objects of cognition are non-existent, they do not arise; this is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
Upon entering the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), this true wisdom that accords with reality perceives that consciousness is non-arising.
Non-arising is suchness itself, and there is no further distinct phenomenon apart from it.
Therefore, taking reality as its essence—such practices are the characteristics for entering the four stages.
The Commentary states: "By means of these skillful means, the bodhisattva is able to enter the four stages."
The following is the fifth section, the explanation of the chapter on entering the path of expedient means (*upāyamārga*).
This refers specifically to the expedient means of the stage of entry (*praveśasthāna-upāya*).

By relying on these four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) together with the fundamental expedient means, one causes cultivation to increase, thereby supporting the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā-bhāvanā*) so that one may attain entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*).
This chapter consists of three parts:
first, the commentary explains the entry into the preparatory means;
second, the inquiry.
Third, the answer:

The *Śāstra* explains the intent of the question by showing that one enters the four stages by taking the eight bases as the support and the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) as the means (*upāya*).
Among these eight bases, the first six serve as the means.
The latter two serve as the provisions (*sambhāra*) and are both causes for entry;
they further demonstrate the meaning of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*).
This is as explained in the chapter on "Entering into People.
Furthermore, within the third of the three responses, it is divided into three parts;
first, the virtuous roots that are upheld are shown.
These are the aforementioned four powers.
Second, it demonstrates that the practice capable of sustaining the roots of goodness has eight points.
Third, it takes these eight points as its focus and provides a detailed explanation thereof.
The root treatise states, "By the power of the sustenance of the roots of goodness.
This clarifies the power of goodness,
which does not exceed four kinds of powers.
Because one maintains these eight points to cause them to increase, the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is accomplished.
The root treatise states: "By means of three aspects for refining the mind," which constitutes three of the eight points.
The elimination of the four obstacles to transformation is the fourth of the eight stages.
Taking the meaning of the Dharma as one's object is the fifth stage.
The uninterrupted cultivation of meditative concentration and wisdom is the sixth.
Venerating concentration and cultivating wisdom constitute the seventh basis;
practicing heedfulness is the eighth basis.
These eight bases are all points for training and cultivation.
By practicing this, one matures the power of the four kinds of roots of goodness.
The eight stages are established through a sequence of increasing depth;
the first three types of mental refinement constitute three [stages].
First, the topical outline is presented;
second, the three types of mental cultivation are explained;
finally, it is further concluded with three verses of practice.
The *Śāstra* further explains this.
The *Śāstra* says: "First, the mind of despondency, such as self-contempt.
This is the third section below, which provides a detailed explanation of the preparatory means (*upāya*).
This clarifies that because awakening is vast, profound, difficult to practice, and difficult to attain upon hearing of it, the mind becomes discouraged.
It is "profound" in terms of its mode of being (*yathābhūta*),
and "vast" in terms of its extent of meaning (*yāvadbhāva*).
It is difficult to practice because it encompasses all phenomena exhaustively.
It is said to be profound because the means for practicing according to the text are attained;
because it is profound, it is difficult to realize.
There are three meanings for treating this mind.
First, it is explained that there is no fixed location;
wherever one can find a conducive place to practice, cultivation may be undertaken.
Second, it clarifies that the human path is an appropriate vessel for this; those of the same class who practice will all attain it.
Third, it clarifies that there is no fixed time limit.
By practicing diligently according to one's capacity, both are attained.
Taking this as an illustration, this training refines the mind and treats the first type of discouraged mind.
The Commentary states: "The second is the discouraged mind that disparages the skillful means capable of attainment."
When a bodhisattva forms this mind,
[he realizes that] giving and the other perfections are the provisions for enlightenment;
yet these cannot be attained apart from the bodhisattva’s intention.
"How can we possibly carry out this practice?"—
this is a mind of despondency. To remedy this mind:
One clearly recognizes that the Bodhisattvas of the three periods are of the same kind as oneself,
all of whom are able to cultivate giving and the other perfections,
taking faith and aspiration as their correct intention.
Right intention serves as the means;
possessing these three meanings, one is able to equally cultivate and grow the six perfections,
and possesses the three kinds of faith and delight.
The three kinds of Buddha-nature are explained in detail according to their meaning in the *Yìzhāng* (Chapter on Meaning).
As for the primary intent, it is the ability to practice the six perfections and so forth,
which fully possesses the three functions of growth, production, and equality.
Because one has emerged from the stains of hindrances,
it is not difficult to practice the deeds such as generosity;
through these correct intentions, the six perfections are fulfilled and enlightenment is naturally attained.
The mind of despondency is thereby extinguished.
The *Śāstra* states that there are three meanings regarding that which is most difficult to obtain.
First, it must be cultivated for a long duration;
second, that which is cultivated must be subtle and refined;
third, that which is cultivated must be manifold.
From the first stage up to the tenth stage, throughout thirty great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of practice, one eliminates all states of birth and death except for the final single moment of mind;
because this is difficult to conceive, one may give rise to despondency and retreat.
In observing the preceding state, there are four kinds of concentrated mind:
first, reflection;
second, comprehension.
Third, realization;
fourth, elimination.
First, one investigates that all phenomena are nothing but consciousness.
Having already engaged in such investigation, one definitively understands that all phenomena are nothing but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Once this has been decisively and clearly understood, one subsequently realizes consciousness-only.
This realization of consciousness-only eliminates external objects but does not yet eliminate the substance of consciousness itself.
Later, upon further reflection, he realized that since objects have no characteristics,
consciousness lacks the necessary causes and conditions to arise.
Furthermore, because he did not perceive the essence of consciousness, he termed this "the elimination of the mind."
This refers to the mind being adjacent to suchness.
Because this mind remains within obstructions, it cannot attain true realization;
yet the mind itself is the path to liberation.
Elimination is the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Beyond this, the subsequent mind and the principle are one, with no distinction between subject and object.
The *Śāstra* says: "One should also be able to attain this meaning, which is difficult to conceive."
There are many virtues and wisdoms that are obstructed;
that which can obstruct the momentary mind of *śamatha* is said to be able to attain this inconceivable meaning.
I am still within the four kinds of birth and death;
my departure from the adamantine state that eliminates the mind is still far off.
Since the obstructions are many, those capable of obstructing should likewise be many.
If one says that this "unattainability" is also inconceivable,
doubt arises and leads to despondency; therefore,
an example is subsequently cited as an antidote for the mind.
It is clear that when ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles cultivate obstructed roots of goodness, they each attain their respective fruits without fail;
how much more so should I now, cultivating perfect and unobstructed goodness, not attain the fruit?
Now, the cultivation of the three categories—generosity, ethical discipline, and meditation—is itself concentration (*samādhi*).
If one merely possesses the essential substance [of these practices] without cultivating all three categories, it is called "partial.
To possess all three categories—namely, the giving of material wealth, the Dharma, and fearlessness—is what constitutes complete cultivation.
One attains the fruit upon casting off life;
by dying and falling [into a lower realm], one immediately transforms from an ordinary being into a sage.
One does not attain a shift of station without casting off life.
The commentary states: "Because one delights in cultivating the two categories of wholesome dharmas—merit and wisdom—within the ten stages, they are called 'perfection' (*paripūri*).
These two meanings are explained from two perspectives:
first, in relation to the various stages (*bhūmi*).
In each stage, the practice of the six perfections is fulfilled;
secondly, fulfillment is achieved through the integration of the ultimate and conventional truths,
wherein ultimate understanding constitutes wisdom.
The conventional interpretation takes this to mean "merit.
Being eternally present and endowed with the four virtues, its sovereignty constitutes "unimpededness.
The meaning of the perfect virtues of the Dharma-body is "abundance and joy."
The response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) benefits others; those who practice the supreme path are able to transform [it] and take this as their practice.
Mastery over the joy of the Dharma serves as its wish-fulfilling power.
The transformation body assumes physical form, meaning, marks and signs, voice, eloquence, and skillful means as its objects of endearment.
The subsequent summary of the intent is easy to understand.
Furthermore, three verses of verse re-summarize the meaning of the three previous refinements of the mind;
they are now clearly manifest and visible.
The meaning of the preceding [verse] is as explained before.
Regarding the explanation of the two lines of the second verse as manifesting three meanings:
the three types of Buddha-nature, which are the objects of faith and aspiration for all supreme bodhisattvas, together serve as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
A wholesome mind serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Generosity and other practices, as well as the supramundane dharmas resulting from the observance of ethical discipline, constitute its outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
As the root treatise states: "Because of the elimination of the four obstructions."
This refers back to the fourth of the eight points mentioned previously:
"removing the four obstacles.
The first is wrong reflection (*mithyā-manasikāra*).
Second, wrong intention and doubt;
third, the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self regarding phenomena;
fourth, the cessation of clear knowledge.
These are the four obstacles in brief.
The *Śāstra* states: "To repeatedly contemplate the faults of saṃsāra and the merits of nirvāṇa is merely the contemplation of those who cherish themselves.
Because their minds engage in conceptual discrimination, they perceive self and other, gain and loss, within the non-dual principle."
Because one cannot treat others with impartiality, it constitutes wrong reflection (*mithyā-manasikāra*).
The second [category], wrong intention (*mithyā-āśaya*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), are both clarified:
because one gives rise to faith and a mind of decisive understanding regarding the principles of the two truths and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), wrong intention and doubt are extinguished.
To understand that within the sphere of hearing and reflection there are no phenomena, yet they arise in accordance with the mind,
while nevertheless grasping at the essence of these phenomena as being existent, is called the clinging to a self of phenomena (*dharmātman-grāha*).
Furthermore, to understand that these phenomena possess functional utility is called the clinging to what belongs to a self of phenomena (*dharma-mamāyita-grāha*).
Furthermore, for example, consider one who maintains that there is nirvana, asserting that its essence is the non-arising and quiescence of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Since the truth of origination is the cause of suffering,
to "exist" would be to arise.
To claim that because there is no arising it is a false attachment—
that is, to take the path of a bodhisattva as the cause for nirvāṇa while treating the cause as the effect.
Is this not a false attachment?
Furthermore, it is like holding that the function of *nirvāṇa* is to enable one to leave behind the three types of suffering;
that which can leave suffering behind is, in fact, the Path.
The path capable of abandoning suffering is the cause of nirvāṇa;
because it can abandon suffering,
nirvāṇa is the fruit.
Furthermore, at the time of the fruit, suffering has already ceased;
to claim that [the path] is only then able to eliminate suffering is to conflate it with the cause.
Is this not a false attachment?
Next, the fourth stage of liberation involves the cessation of conceptual grasping.
It clarifies that both concentration and distraction take internal objects as their focus rather than external ones;
because one perceives that objects are signless and consciousness is unborn, one is able to extinguish conceptualization.
This section consists of both prose and verse.
The subsequent verse commentary does not differ from what preceded it.
The root treatise states: "Taking the meaning of conditions as the object."
Among these eight points, regarding the fifth:
as the *Śāstra* (Commentary) cites the preceding treatise to establish it as a formal heading (*dharmamukha*), it then provides an explanation through question and answer.
It answers the first question by stating that the "hearing-perfuming" (*śrutavāsanā*) serves as the cause for its arising.
Reflective wisdom (*cintāmayī prajñā*) is the primary cause; this is the expedient means for answering the second question.

Subsequently, when wisdom such as reflection arises, it relies upon this wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) and repeatedly contemplates it as the primary factor, causing it to remain firm; therefore, it is said to be "comprised" [within it].
Right reflection is the primary cause; alternatively,
that which resembles the authentic teaching serves as the object of the wisdom arising from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*),
while that which appears as the meaning realized by the authentic teaching serves as the object of the wisdom arising from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
It is explained later that subsequent illumination, observation, and reflection are precisely mental verbal discrimination (*manojalpa-vikalpa*).
Furthermore, there is the perception of what is to be understood.

The root treatise states: "By means of four kinds of investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*), namely, the investigation into the designation (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*), the object (*artha-paryeṣaṇā*), the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-paryeṣaṇā*), and the specific difference (*viśeṣa-paryeṣaṇā*) through conventional designation (*prajñapti*)."
This is the sixth of the eight bases.
It is uninterrupted cultivation;
it receives the name "uninterrupted" because of this.

Because the continuity of the practice of increasingly superior skillful means is uninterrupted by evil or neutral states that would intervene between wholesome states, it is called "uninterrupted cultivation" (*nirantara-bhāvanā*).
This is based on both the name and its meaning.
Regarding the fourfold establishment of names, objects, intrinsic natures, and distinctions of names and objects:
that which can designate all things is called "name" (nāma);
that which is designated—namely, all phenomena such as the six consciousnesses, their objects, and the eighteen elements—is called "object" (artha).
Regarding the intrinsic nature of name and referent:
these two, name and referent, have mere verbal expression as their intrinsic nature.
As for their distinction:
As it is said, the five aggregates and eighteen elements are the establishment of names and meanings.
Names and meanings constitute the fundamental basis, while the various meanings serve as their distinctions.
For example, form, sensation, and so forth are each distinct from one another by virtue of their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Within each aggregate (skandha) and each element (dhātu), there are further various distinctions;
just as there are diverse forms within form,
so it is with all things.
It is called the discourse of differentiation.
Since there is nothing other than the discourse that perceives the intrinsic nature of names and objects, it is said that discourse constitutes its intrinsic nature.
Regarding the phrase "only seeing the verbal expression of the differentiation between name and referent":
"name and referent" refers to the actual entities themselves,
while "differentiation" refers to their specific distinctions.
Since the essence of these [objects] consists in expressing their specific meanings through verbal discourse, they too exist only as verbal discourse.
The thorough investigation (*vitarka*) that resolves doubts regarding the four bases is designated as "discernment" (*vicāra*).
Because both of these take mere conventional verbal expression as their object, the remaining three [investigations] are established as being "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) with them.
The meaning of "three eyes" (trimukha) is equivalent to the meaning of "belonging to.

Because one generates understanding through the sequential continuity of practicing the three [trainings], it is called "associated" (yoga); it is so named because the conceptual construction of dharmas arises from that understanding.
Regarding the statement that "name and object are mutually adventitious":
when one apprehends an object, one has not yet recognized its name;
it is like seeing a person without recognizing their nature.
Therefore, we know they are not identical because names are many.
Just as a single person has many names but does not have many bodies, we know that [the dharmas] do not have multiple identities.
Because the three names are not fixed,
and because one knows that the person is like a son and so forth, they do not constitute a single entity.
Furthermore, a single name may denote multiple meanings.
As in the previous enumeration, this is the ninth;
therefore, they are not the same. This clarifies that they are different at one and the same time.
Furthermore, a name is established only after there has first been a person;
likewise, one knows that after the path of humans exists as described in the text, this path is subsequently named "the human path.
This applies generally to all preceding texts where the person is determinately established first, and only thereafter does the person exist.
This clarifies the difference between the preceding and the subsequent.
Furthermore, one may know this person’s name and surname from a text, yet not recognize that person’s physical form;
therefore, name and meaning differ in substance.
Next is the analogy of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Just as the five aggregates are a collection of formations (*saṃskāra-rāśi*) and thus bear the name "impermanent," yet within this continuity there remains the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
Thus, one knows that while the name is impermanent, it is as if the meaning were conceived as permanent;
therefore, one knows they do not share the same substance.
For this reason, it is said that name and meaning are mutually guests to one another.
However, if one does not repeatedly practice these three meanings in their proper sequence and without inversion, there can be no sense of "correspondence" (saṃprayoga).
To clarify this meaning and demonstrate its distinctions, it is said that because each is distinct and the individual factors are separate, they are impermanent; thus, this teaching exists.

The root treatise states: "By means of four kinds of knowledge as it truly is—namely, the knowledge as it truly is of names, meanings, intrinsic nature, and distinctions—one does not perceive these four.
The following section clarifies the sixth provision.
The chapter is divided into three sections:
first, the exposition on cultivation through reverence;
second, the exposition on cultivation through heedfulness.
Third, resolving doubts and distinguishing the dwelling place and its objective sphere.
First, the clarification of the three aspects of respectful cultivation.
Within this, the first part clarifies the four types of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Second, the contemplation of the skillful means of Vijñapti-mātra;
third, the true contemplation of Vijñapti-mātra.
Regarding the first, within the four types of actual wisdom, there are again three.
First, the general introduction;
second, the detailed explanation of each individual point;
third, the general conclusion and summary.
The investigation through reasoning and the knowledge of reality both occur at the moment of emergence from the final mind of the tenth stage of reversal;
they also occur during the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of all the grounds as one is about to enter those stages.
Investigation (vitarka) occurs at the stages of Heat (uṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan);
knowledge according to reality (yathābhūtajñāna) occurs at the stages of Patience (kṣānti) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
Nevertheless, both of these chapters may be considered as the preparatory equipment for the means (upāya-saṃbhāra).
Now, taking up True Contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*):
that which is distant serves as the skillful means (*upāya*),
while that which is proximate serves as the provision (*sambhāra*).

However, while the four preceding investigations (paryeṣaṇā) know that these four are merely conventional designations, they have not yet reached the realization that the four dharmas do not exist at all.

Because one can now clearly realize that the four dharmas truly do not exist and are unattainable, the four kinds of knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūtaparijñāna) are established. Next, the individual explanations follow.
First, regarding the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by thorough investigation:
it is in fact for the sake of leading sentient beings to the supramundane that the names of the myriad things of the world are established.
If these names were not established, no one would recognize phenomena such as form and so forth.
Consequently, they cannot give rise to the grasping of superimposition;
even when instructing one another,
how could they possibly understand the principle of transcending the world?
Therefore, one borrows worldly dharmas to lead others toward the supramundane.
As previously explained in the section on entering the basis, the two aspects of persons and dharmas— both general and specific—
are entirely provisional borrowings intended solely as means for entering into the realization of the principle.
All are entirely non-existent.
Next, the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of meaning,
clarifies that meaning is free from all verbal expression and is inexpressible.
Next, to clarify that which is not form (*arūpa*): it has no substantial entity and is inexpressible.
It is not said that form appears as if it were form;
the same applies to the existence or non-existence of phenomena that are not form.
Because the Dharma has three meanings that are inexpressible,
this is the second [type of] knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Next,
thirdly, there is the investigation of the verbal expression of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vyavahāra-paryeṣaṇā*).
There is only verbal expression;
by virtue of verbal expression regarding intrinsic nature, this class is not its intrinsic nature,
even though it appears as if it were its intrinsic nature.
The Bodhisattva understands that these are like illusions, transformations, and so forth;
they do not manifest as something truly similar to their appearance.
This is called the third knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the profound meaning is the object," this refers to taking the signless (*animitta*) and the dependent cognition (*paratantra-vijñāna*) as the object.
Next, the fourth distinction is explained: that there are no two meanings in verbal expression.
This clarifies that all distinctions between names and meanings in verbal expression are non-dual.
Because both the speech and that which is expressed are entirely non-existent, they are non-dual.
Since the substance of what can be expressed is not established, it is the nature of conceptual construction (parikalpita-svabhāva) that lacks intrinsic reality.
Because it is matured as an ineffable essence, it is the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Next, the non-duality of differentiated verbal expressions constitutes the fourth [type of] knowledge of things-as-they-are (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
Following this, the four meanings are explained in general, based on what was previously stated regarding names and their referents.
This is a summary: clear wisdom is conventional designation;
the investigation that transcends doubt and brings definitive understanding is called "investigation" (*vitarka*).
Based on this investigation, the bodhisattva contemplates that both name and referent are non-existent; this is "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Next, "having entered this" refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the contemplation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The four kinds of roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), which serve as the basis, are the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
The subsequent text explains this itself.
Next, the sequence clarifies the non-perception of the self-nature and distinctions of names and meanings;
it can be understood by relying on the commentary.

Having used the four thorough investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four kinds of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) as the two skillful means to dispel external objects, what further skillful means and objective domain are required to enter true contemplation (*tattvadarśana*)?
This concludes the third question below, concerning the true contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The preceding was merely an understanding that resembles the skillful means;
one must now investigate this further to enter into reality.
Because the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) discriminates these four dharmas, they arise; yet these four dharmas are ultimately non-existent.
When mental discourse and all conditions for further conceptualization have been exhausted,
the consciousness of mental-discourse discrimination can no longer arise;
this is precisely the entry into true contemplation.
Furthermore, seeing the nature of signlessness is true seeing;
realizing that there is only consciousness and that all other phenomena are entirely non-existent is called entering the contemplation of ultimate reality (*tattva*).
As for the four kinds of samādhi:
These four are the bases for the four contemplations within the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*);
they are not the four types of skillful means— namely, *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*— within the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
This refers to first attaining the four dhyānas, such as the "equal" (samatā) dhyāna and so forth;
these will be explained in their own chapter later.
The Commentary states:
The following clarifies the eighth of the eight points:
the cultivation of heedfulness;
this constitutes the second section of the chapter.
Regarding this, there is a question and answer.
This dialogue clarifies both the doctrinal and analogical explanations,
which are divided into two sections.
First, the teaching by way of the Dharma;
second, the teaching by way of analogy.
Within the teaching by way of the Dharma, there are two parts.
First, a brief indication of the intent regarding the cognition of the three means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
second, an extensive explanation of the meaning of the three means of valid knowledge.
The root treatise states: "Those who enter merely into the measure-only (*pramāṇa-mātra*)."
This clarifies that through conventional observation, the nature of consciousness alone is established as the reality.
Although various aspects of the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) are subsequently explained,

if these two— the image and the seeing— as well as their manifold varieties were not transformations occurring upon consciousness itself without inversion, then the principle of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) would not be established.
Because consciousness cannot arise without the condition of the arising of the non-perceiving [subject],
if there were truly existent form, the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) would not be established;
for although it transforms into duality, it lacks a dual essence and is but a single reality.
The Commentary states: Regarding these two dharmas, one is the cause and the other is the fruit.
The object (*viṣaya*) is the cause;
thus, the meaning of "arising" is established, and yet the consciousness that apprehends the grasper and the grasped is not lost.
Consciousness is the effect;
this is stated with respect to the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The sense-faculties (indriya) are the cause of consciousness.
Consciousness is the fruit;
this is explained in terms of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If, however, it is considered in terms of the sense of transformation (*vipariṇāma*), [it is as follows].
Consciousness is the cause;
the faculties and objects are both the effects,
for the faculties and objects arise from the seeds of consciousness as their causal conditions.
