This is because, apart from consciousness, there would be no objects such as forms and so forth.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, one is the support and one is the supported.
The sense organs and their objects are the support.
Consciousness is that which depends [on others].
From the transformation of consciousness, seeds arise as the sense faculties and their objects;
thus, it can also be said that the sense faculties and their objects are that which depend [on consciousness].
Consciousness is the basis.
The Commentary states: "Because these two dharmas have been repeatedly practiced since beginningless saṃsāra, they are swift; therefore, at one time, various appearances arise."
If one proceeds according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), taking consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) as the ultimate measure,
then in order to establish the meaning of consciousness, it is opened up into the two phenomena of the grasped aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the grasping aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
Extensively speaking, there are six consciousnesses as the grasper and six sense objects (*viṣaya*) as the grasped.
Because each possesses immeasurable particles of consciousness, they are said to have "various characteristics.
Whether discussing the eight consciousnesses arising simultaneously or sequentially, their distinctions are infinitely manifold.
Although they appear as various types, in reality, they are nothing but the measure of consciousness itself.
The Commentary states: "The names and meanings each have three, making six.

From this point downward, the second part of the main treatise provides a further detailed explanation of the Dharma-discourse on meaning, correctly clarifying that the entry into consciousness consists of only three types of contemplation.
First, regarding the clarification of "representation-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), the six aspects constitute its meaning.
Next, concerning the statement "seeking the name, nothing is found":
since the name originally refers to the object (*artha*), and that object does not exist, it is called "the non-existence of the object."
The causes are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), which constitute their referent.
Since these sense objects do not exist, this is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
What is the meaning of "having no cause"?

Furthermore, regarding this term "non-existence" (*abhāva*), does it have an intrinsic meaning or is it devoid of meaning? If it has a meaning, yet that meaning is non-existent, it is therefore called "non-existence.
If one were to exclude an existing entity, there could be a "non-existence" belonging to that which exists.
Since there is no existence within the phenomenon of existence,
how could there be the non-existence of that house?
Therefore, this [position] is also devoid of meaning.
Next, the two dharmas of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and differentiation (*viśeṣa*) are as can be seen in the commentary;
they are not explained here.
Next, the second [section], which clarifies the manifestation of the characteristics and the vision, is explained according to the commentary.
Since the meaning of establishing the grasped and the grasper has thus failed to be established,
one finally realizes that within a single consciousness there exist the two phenomena of the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*), which are produced by one's own conceptual differentiation.
Next, the third commentary on the *Triṃśikā* explains the contemplation of various appearances as follows:
In a single moment, one can contemplate various characteristics;
that which is signless and unarisen is called "entering into various characteristics.
For the contemplator, the signless and the unarisen constitute the foundation.
From the Dharma one arrives at the ultimate limit of the fundamental nature of phenomena; only then does one reach the accomplishment of the contemplation of their various characteristics.
If one does not penetrate the essence of principle, then even if one understands inverted phenomenal appearances, such understanding will ultimately never become a correct understanding.
Next, the explanation of the analogies for entering the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) answers the second question, "How [does one enter]? This is further divided into two parts.
First, there are thirty-four lines of text which explain the analogy and its application through a combined interpretation.
Second, from this point, based on the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which appears as objects, the following thirty-three lines of prose explain and establish the preceding analogy;
that is, the analogy borrows the phenomena of the Hīnayāna to serve as its illustration.
For example, it is like failing to discern a vine in the dark and mistaking it for a snake.
The snake represents the fact that the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) exists within the dependent nature;
the vine represents that consciousness exists within the conventional reality.
This is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
When the rope is examined through its constituent objects, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and consists only of the four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*).
These four subtle elements serve as an analogy for the true nature (*tathatā*) within the established nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
However, the snake was originally non-existent;
it was due to darkness that one failed to perceive the vine and, seeing it lying across [the path], mistakenly took it for a snake.
In the same way, all sentient beings fail to discern that within the conventional world there is nothing but consciousness.
One forms the conceptualization of sense organs, objects, and so forth upon consciousness;
yet these organs and objects truly do not exist,
just as there is fundamentally no snake upon a vine.
Next, it is explained that the creeper has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
The four subtle elements (paramāṇu) are conventionally designated as the creeper;
however, when one realizes the four subtle elements, the creeper is no longer perceived to exist.
For example, just as one who does not realize that within reality all is of one suchness and signless,
perceives the nature of the root and objects through the inverted views described above—
just as when seeing a snake, one does not see the vine.
Since the sense faculties and their objects are both non-existent,
one perceives the nature of signlessness;
this refers to the aspect of the non-existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
To perceive suchness and to perceive that there is only consciousness is to perceive the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva);
it is like perceiving that there is no snake when one perceives the rope.
If one does not yet understand that consciousness arises conditioned by the four subtle elements, then there is no vision of non-arising and no vision of signlessness;
this non-arising is precisely the conventional consciousness seeing true reality.
It is like when one sees the four subtle elements, there is no [separate] vine.
Originally, True Suchness was established in contrast to conventional consciousness;
since the conventional is empty and has nothing to contrast with,
the True is likewise free from all dependence— the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
Just as when one sees the four subtle particles, they too are non-existent and are merely emptiness;
this is the perfection of the nature of reality as being without intrinsic nature,
which is the unestablished truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
There is no [distinction] regarding the two truths or the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The root treatise states: "In this way, by entering into that which appears as objects...
and so forth. This second explanation in terms of phenomena further clarifies the preceding analogy.

Apart from the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna true teaching, it cannot be understood;
apart from non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it cannot be extinguished.
This is the subtle seed of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*).
Because all defiled phenomena depend upon this as their causal condition for arising, it is called "defiled phenomena" (*saṃkleśa*).
Because an immeasurable collection of seeds resides within this basis, it is called "dense" (*gahana*).
Because it is entirely non-different in essence from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and cannot be distinguished from it, it is called "secret" (*guhya*).
The Commentary states: "As for the *agada* medicine," this refers to the absence of medicine.
This medicine can cure all diseases;
just as a wish-fulfilling jewel can eliminate everything,
so too can this [medicine] eliminate all illnesses.
It may be called the priceless excellent medicine;
it is also the incomparable excellent medicine.
The *Śāstra* says: "The reason for this is that both the principle taught and the fruit attained are supreme."
The principle of the One Vehicle consists of such doctrines as the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
As for the fruit, it is Great Nirvāṇa that is supreme.
Furthermore, it clarifies that within the three vehicles, the Bodhisattva is "Great" because they encompass the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, one attains the great by depending on the small;
however, as for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), there is neither two nor three vehicles because it is solely one.
A vehicle that is without mutual dependence is the truly supreme vehicle.
Non-conceptual wisdom takes the dharma-realm as its root;
its essence is the faculty of knowledge,
because it arises from the faculties of the known and the unknown.
It is also called "possessing faculties" (*saindriya*).
The faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) arises from knowledge according to reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the treatise states that it is also called "possessing faculties" because it arises from the causal condition of the nature of understanding (*avabodha-dhātu*).
Because it can produce subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and further advance the subsequently attained applied knowledge (*prṣṭhalabdha-prayoga-jñāna*),
it is also called "possessing roots" (*sāmūlaka*).
It is called "possessing roots" because it possesses its own essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Why is this so? Because by attaining this wisdom, other forms of wisdom are extinguished;
and because wisdom relies upon this wisdom to further give rise to the merit and wisdom of the higher stages, it is therefore called a faculty (*indriya*).
